profileDesc.creation:
Initially created: 2025-12-06T13:37:34.685+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.
Input text:

p.seg: On this day,
the Khitan ruler led his troops from Chìgāng into the palace,
entering the Jìn palace.
All were guarded by Khitan soldiers,
who day and night did not lay down their weapons.
They feared a mutiny.
They hung a sheepskin on a pole in the courtyard as a talisman to ward off evil.
The Khitan ruler said to
his ministers:
"From now on, we shall not repair armor or weapons,
nor purchase warhorses.
We will lighten taxes and reduce corvée labor,
and all under heaven will be at peace."
Easier said than done!
These words had barely left his mouth,
when the "grass and grain levies" followed.
Was all under heaven truly at peace?
He demoted the Kāifēng Prefecture to Biànzhōu,
and its governor to a defense commissioner.
On the yǐwèi day,
the Khitan ruler changed into Central Plains attire,
and the rituals for the hundred officials' daily greetings were all as per the old system.
History records that the Khitan ruler still knew to use Xià ways to transform the barbarians.
Zhào Yánshòu and Zhāng Lì together recommended Lǐ Sōng's talent;
it happened that Wēishèng Military Commissioner Féng Dào came to court from Dèngzhōu.
The Khitan ruler had long heard of these two men's reputations,
and treated them both with courtesy and respect.
These two men had served through the Táng and Jìn dynasties,
reaching the highest ranks among subjects.
When their state perished, they could not die for it,
viewing their ruler as a mere passerby.
How were they worthy of respect!
He appointed Sōng as Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince,
and concurrently Chief of the Bureau of Military Affairs;
Dào was appointed Grand Preceptor,
and kept in attendance at the Bureau of Military Affairs,
to serve as an advisor.
The Khitan ruler dispatched envoys separately,
bearing edicts to bestow upon Jìn's regional military governors;
Jìn's regional military governors vied to submit memorials declaring themselves subjects,
and those summoned all rushed to arrive.
Only Zhāngyì Military Commissioner Shǐ Kuāngwēi, based in Jīngzhōu, did not accept the command.
Kuāngwēi
was the son of Shǐ Jiàntáng.
Shǐ Jiàntáng served Jìn Prince Lǐ Kèyòng and later Zhuāngzōng,
and had achievements in battle.
He surrendered Qín, Jiē, and Chéng prefectures to Shǔ.
Shǐ Kuāngwēi did not surrender to the Khitan,
because his territory was distant,
and the Khitan's military might could not reach it.
Hé Chóngjiàn, because his commandery bordered Shǔ,
then abandoned the Liáo and attached himself to Shǔ.
Earlier,
Dù Chóngwēi had surrendered the Jìn army to the Khitan.
Dù Chóngwēi initially avoided the Jìn ruler Chóngguì's name taboo,
removing
"Chóng",
and used the single name
"Wēi".
After Jìn perished,
Chóngwēi immediately restored his old name;
his ingratitude and betrayal of his lord,
this was merely a minor detail.
He drove tens of thousands of horses back to his own state,
and sent Chóngwēi to lead his troops to follow him south.
When they reached the river,
the Khitan ruler, due to the large number of Jìn troops,
feared they would mutiny,
and wanted to use Khitan cavalry to surround them and push them into the river's current.
Someone admonished him:
"There are still many Jìn troops elsewhere.
If they hear that those who surrendered were all killed,
they will certainly all resist orders.
It would be better to pacify them for now,
and slowly consider a strategy."
The Khitan ruler then had Chóngwēi station his troops at Chénqiáo.
Chénqiáo was outside Chénqiáo Gate,
and had a Chénqiáo postal station.
The authorities provided no supplies,
and the soldiers suffered from cold and hunger.
They all resented Chóngwēi,
gathering together and weeping;
whenever Chóngwēi went out,
people along the road all cursed him.
The Khitan ruler still wanted to execute the Jìn troops.
Zhào Yánshòu spoke to the Khitan ruler:
"Your Majesty personally braved arrows and stones to capture the Jìn state.
Do you intend to possess it yourself,
or will you let others take it?"
The Khitan ruler's expression changed:
"I mobilized the entire state for a southern campaign,
not removing my armor for five years.
In the eighth year of Tiānfú,
the Khitan began attacking Jìn,
and it has been five years until now.
How could it be for others!"
Hearing the Khitan ruler say this,
Zhào Yánshòu could abandon hope.
"To the south of the Jìn state is Táng,
to the west is Shǔ,
often enemies.
Does Your Majesty know this?"
He said:
"I know."
Yánshòu said:
"The Jìn state stretches east from Yí and Mì,
west to Qín and Fèng,
extending for several thousand lǐ,
bordering Wú and Shǔ,
and often must garrison troops there.
The south is hot and humid,
people from the Upper State cannot live there.
At that time, those holding regional power called the Central Plains the Upper State.
Jìn served the Khitan,
and also called the Khitan the Upper State.
With the Jìn state so vast,
if there are no troops to guard it,
Wú and Shǔ will certainly join forces to invade when it is vulnerable.
If so,
would that not be letting others take it?"
The Khitan ruler said:
"I did not know this.
Then what should be done?"
Yánshòu said:
"The surrendered troops at Chénqiáo
can be divided to garrison the southern border.
Then Wú and Shǔ cannot cause trouble."
The Khitan ruler said:
"In the past at Shàngdǎng,
I erred in not making a decisive cut,
and gave all the Táng troops to Jìn.
This matter is recorded in the 280th scroll, Jìn Gāozǔ Tiānfú first year.
Duàn,
Dīng luàn fān.
They turned north and fought me,
toiling hard for years,
and I barely defeated them.
Now that they have fortunately fallen into my hands,
if I do not take this opportunity to eliminate them all,
how can I leave them to become a future calamity?"
Yánshòu said:
"Previously, Jìn troops were left south of the river,
without their wives and children held as hostages,
hence this worry arose.
Now if we move all their families to the regions between Héng, Dìng, Yún, and Shuò,
and have them take turns garrisoning the southern border each year,
what worry is there of them mutinying?
This is the best strategy."
The Khitan ruler happily said:
"Good!
It is up to you, Great King, to handle it."
The Khitan had enfeoffed Zhào Yánshòu as Prince of Yān,
hence he was called Great King.
Chǔ,
Chāng lǚ fān.
They were sent back to their camps separately.
6 The Khitan ruler executed Right Imperial Guard General-in-Chief Lǐ Yǎnshēn and eunuch Qín Jìmín,
because they had killed the Prince of Eastern Dān for the Táng Prince of Lù.
The killing of the Prince of Eastern Dān is recorded in the 280th scroll, Jìn Gāozǔ Tiānfú first year,
which was the third year of Táng Prince of Lù's Qīngtài era.
Wèi,
Yú wèi fān.
Wùyù was blind in one eye,
and was a robust and generous man.
Wùyù first appears here,
setting the stage for his later gaining the state.
Shī,
Shì chǐ fān.
7 On the guǐmǎo day,
the Jìn ruler, along with Empress Dowager Lǐ, Empress Dowager Ān, Empress Féng, his younger brother Ruì, and sons Yánxù and Yánbǎo, all moved north.
Over a hundred attendants from the inner palace followed.
The Khitan sent three hundred cavalry to escort them;
escort means accompanying their journey to provide protection.
The Jìn ruler on the road
had insufficient provisions,
and sometimes he and the empress dowager both went without food.
None of the old ministers dared to pay their respects.
Only Cízhōu Prefect Lǐ Gǔ met and paid respects on the road,
and they wept facing each other.
Gǔ said:
"I, your subject, am without merit,
and have failed Your Majesty."
Then he offered all his wealth.
Scholars under heaven,
if they have failed in some way,
their actions will certainly differ from others.
Cí,
Qiáng zhī fān.
The Jin ruler arrived at Zhōngdù Bridge,
saw Dù Chóngwēi's camp,
and sighed, saying:
"Heaven!
What wrong has my house committed,
to be destroyed by this traitor!"
He wept bitterly and departed.
During the Jin period,
the entire nation, high and low, all knew that Dù Chóngwēi was unfit for use,
yet they went against the multitude and employed him, leading to the state's destruction.
The Book of Songs says:
"They sob and weep,
but what use is lamenting now?"
Now it has reached the point of bitter weeping,
is there still time for regret?
8 On Guǐchǒu,
the Shǔ ruler appointed Left Thousand Ox Guards Senior General Lǐ Jìxūn as the Pacification Commissioner of Qínzhōu.
Shǔ, because Hé Chóngjiàn had surrendered,
sent an envoy to pacify him.
9 The Khitan ruler appointed former Yānjīng Garrison Commander Liú Xī as Xījīng Garrison Commander.
The Old History of the Five Dynasties says: Liú Xī was
a man of Zhuōzhōu,
who fell captive to the barbarians,
and rose through the ranks to become Grand Councilor and concurrently Palace Attendant.
Textual Analysis says: The Veritable Records writes
"Xǐ".
Some say his name was Xī.
I now follow the Record of Falling Among the Barbarians.
Wùyù's brother-in-law Pān Yùniǎn was appointed Military Commissioner of Hénghǎi,
Zhào Yánshòu's son Kuāngzàn was appointed Military Commissioner of Hùguó,
setting the stage for Zhào Kuāngzàn later surrendering Hézhōng to Hàn.
Shǐ Quán was appointed Military Commissioner of Zhāngyì,
Deputy Commissioner of Guests Liú Yànsēng was appointed Military Commissioner of Zhōngwǔ,
former Military Commissioner of Hùguó Hóu Yì was appointed Military Commissioner of Fèngxiáng,
Acting Prefect of Fèngxiáng Prefecture
Hóu Yì later also surrendered Fèngxiáng to Hàn.
Xī
was a man of Zhuōzhōu.
Subsequently, Hé Chóngjiàn attached himself to Shǔ,
Qínzhōu attached itself to Shǔ,
and Zhāng Yànchāo had nowhere to go.
Shǐ Kuāngwēi occupied Jīngzhōu to resist Shǐ Quán.
10 Military Commissioner of Jìnchāng Zhào Zàilǐ came to court,
from Cháng'ān to court at Dàliáng.
Deputy Military Commissioner Jiànrén Lǐ Sù attacked and executed him,
and the military prefecture was pacified.
11 When the Jin ruler severed relations with the Khitans,
the event is recorded in the 283rd scroll, seventh year of the Tiānfú era of Jin Gāozǔ.
he was quite involved in the planning;
when the Khitan ruler entered Biàn,
Jìxūn came to court,
and the Khitan ruler reprimanded him.
At that time, Féng Dào was in the hall,
and Jìxūn urgently pointed at Dào and said:
"Féng Dào was the chief minister,
and it was he and Jǐng Yánguǎng who actually devised this plan.
My position was lowly,
how dare I speak out!"
The Khitan ruler said:
"This old man is not a busybody,
do not recklessly implicate him!"
Féng Dào avoided disaster by being accommodating;
those who possess a state,
what use do they have for such ministers!
Yet he served seven surnames,
and was always treated with respect due to his virtue and reputation,
also because he conducted himself with caution and composure,
having something that moved their hearts to respect him.
He was to be sent to Huánglóng Prefecture.
Zhào Zàilǐ arrived in Luòyáng,
Old Book of Tang, Treatise on Geography: From Cháng'ān east to Luòyáng is 850 li.
"The Khitan ruler once said the disorder during Zhuāngzōng's reign was caused by me.
Referring to the rebellion of Huángfǔ Huī.
The event is recorded in the 274th scroll, first year of the Tiānchéng era of Táng Míngzōng,
which was the fourth year of Zhuāngzōng's Tóngguāng era.
The Khitans dispatched Khitan general Shùzhá,
writing 'Khitan general'
to distinguish him from Hàn generals and Bóhǎi generals.
Bóhǎi general Gāo Móhàn garrisoned Luòyáng,
Zàilǐ entered for an audience,
bowed in the courtyard below,
and the Yìlà and others all sat sprawled out to receive it.
On Yǐmǎo,
Zàilǐ reached Zhèngzhōu,
Jiǔyù Zhì: From Luòyáng east to Zhèngzhōu is 260 li.
was greatly alarmed,
and at night,
hanged himself in the horse stable.
When the Khitan ruler heard of Zàilǐ's death,
he then released Jìxūn,
and Jìxūn died of grief and indignation.
Liú Xī, while among the Khitans, had once served as Privy Councilor and Grand Councilor,
and upon reaching Luòyáng,
berated the Xī king, saying:
"Zhào Zàilǐ was a great minister of the Hàn house,
you are merely a northern chieftain,
how can you treat him with such disrespect!"
He stood in the courtyard below to humble him.
From then on, the people of Luòyáng became slightly more at ease.
The Khitan ruler extensively received tributes from all directions,
indulged greatly in drinking and merrymaking,
and often said to the Jin ministers:
"Regarding the affairs of the Central Plains,
I know them all,
but the affairs of our country,
you all do not know."
The Khitan ruler boasted to the Jin ministers about the tightness of his own precautions.
However, the coming of Dōngdān
had already planted the seed of the disaster where Wùyù would seize the state,
even the most foolish knew it,
but the Khitan ruler did not.
Those skilled at observing states
do not look at their momentary strength or weakness, but observe the general state of their order or disorder.
Zhào Yánshòu requested provisions for the troops of the superior state,
the Khitan ruler said:
"Our country has no such method."
He then let the Hu cavalry roam out in all directions,
under the pretext of pasturing horses,
taking turns plundering,
calling it
"cutting grass and grain."
Able-bodied men perished by blade and spear,
the old and weak were abandoned in ditches and gullies,
from the two capital regions, east and west
Dàliáng's subordinate counties were the Eastern Capital Region,
Luòyáng's subordinate counties were the Western Capital Region,
this was the Táng system.
Under the Táng system,
the two capitals, aside from the capital counties,
the remaining subordinate counties were capital region counties.
For several hundred li around,
wealth and livestock were nearly exhausted.
Zhèng, Huá, Cáo, Pú,
were all commanderies adjacent to Dàliáng,
mentioned here to clarify
that the so-called Eastern and Western Capital Regions in the text above refer to the capital region counties.
Pú,
Bómù fān.
The Khitan ruler said to Judge of the Three Departments Liú Xù:
"The Khitan army of 300,000,
having now pacified the Jin state,
deserves generous rewards,
you should quickly prepare them."
At that time, the treasury was empty and exhausted,
Xù did not know where to get them from,
so he requested to levy loans of money and silk from the gentry and commoners of the capital city,
the capital city,
meaning the capital city of Dàliáng.
He also separately dispatched several dozen envoys to the various prefectures to levy loans,
all enforced with severe punishments,
so that people had no means to live.
In reality, nothing was distributed as rewards,
it was all stored in the inner treasury,
intending to cart it back to their own country.
Consequently, resentment and indignation arose both inside and out,
people began to suffer and resent the Khitans,
and all thought of driving them out.
This sets the stage for the Khitans returning north.
12 Initially,
the Jin ruler and the Military Commissioner of Hédōng, Secretariat Director, Prince of Běipíng Liú Zhīyuǎn were suspicious and jealous of each other.
Although he was appointed Commander-in-Chief of the Northern Front Field Headquarters,
it was merely honoring him with an empty title,
and regarding the advance or halt of the various armies,
he actually had no part in the decisions.
The event is recorded in the 284th scroll, first year of the Kāiyùn era of Jin Prince of Qí.
In the eighth year of Tiānfú,
when Prince of Qí first created a rift with the Khitans,
Liú Zhīyuǎn had already memorialized to recruit troops,
the event is recorded in the 283rd scroll.
Several thousand scattered soldiers from the various armies returned to him,
the battle of Yángchéng is recorded in the 284th scroll, second year of the Kāiyùn era of Jin Prince of Qí.
According to the battle of Yángchéng,
the Jin army achieved a great victory,
there is no reason for scattered soldiers to return to Hédōng,
this must have been when Dù Chóngwēi surrendered to the Khitans.
The event is also recorded in the second year of Kāiyùn.
Xù,
Xūyù fān.
Infantry and cavalry reached fifty thousand men.
The ruler of Jìn had formed enmity with the Khitan,
and Liú Zhīyuǎn knew that this would inevitably lead to peril,
yet he never remonstrated or advised against it.
The Khitan repeatedly made deep incursions,
but Zhīyuǎn initially had no intention of intercepting them or sending troops to provide relief.
He neither occupied strategic passes and strongholds to intercept the Khitan army,
nor did he dispatch troops to provide relief.
Zhīyuǎn divided his forces to guard the four borders to prevent invasion and raids.
He sent his guest general Wáng Jùn from Ānyáng
(Old Book of Táng, Treatise on Geography: Xiàngzhōu,
was the Hàn and Wèi commandery,
with its seat at Ānyáng County.
Ānyáng,
a marquisate in Hàn times,
its old city was east of Tāngyīn.
During the Cáo Wèi period,
Ānyáng was abolished,
and merged into Yè.
Later, Zhōu moved Yè,
established a county at the old city of Ānyáng,
which was still called Yè County.
Suí again changed it to Ānyáng County,
the seat of the prefecture.
The city of the Hàn and Wèi commandery was about seven lǐ northwest of the county seat.)
General,
read as "jiàng".
to congratulate [the Khitan] on entering Biàn;
second,
because Tàiyuán had a mixed population of barbarians and Chinese,
and was a gathering place for garrison troops,
he dared not leave his post;
third,
because he should have presented tribute,
but it happened that the Khitan general Liú Jiǔyī's army had entered from Tǔmén in the west and was stationed at Nánchuān,
(Nánchuān,
refers to the land south of Jìnyáng city.)
and he was waiting for this army to be recalled,
so that the roads would be clear,
and he could then present tribute.
The Khitan ruler bestowed an edict praising him,
and when presenting the document,
personally added
the character "son"
above Zhīyuǎn's name,
and also bestowed upon him a wooden staff.
According to barbarian custom,
when showing special favor to a high minister, it was bestowed,
similar to the Hàn practice of bestowing small tables and staffs,
only Wěi Wáng, due to his尊 status as an uncle, had received one.
Zhīyuǎn also sent Běidū deputy留守 Bái Wénkē from Tàiyuán to present rare silks and famous horses,
but the Khitan ruler knew that Zhīyuǎn was watching and waiting and would not come,
and when Wénkē returned,
had him say to Zhīyuǎn:
"You do not serve the Southern Court,
nor do you serve the Northern Court,
what are you waiting for?"
The barbarian-Chinese孔目官 Guō Wēi said to Zhīyuǎn:
"The barbarians hate us deeply!
Wáng Jùn said the Khitan are greedy and cruel and have lost the people's hearts,
they certainly cannot long possess the Central Plains."
Some urged Zhīyuǎn to raise troops and advance to seize territory.
Zhīyuǎn said:
"The use of troops has its slow and urgent moments,
one must adapt to the times.
Now the Khitan have recently subdued a hundred thousand Jìn troops,
and are firmly entrenched in the capital,
with no other changes,
how can we act lightly!
Moreover, I observe that what they desire is limited to goods and wealth,
once they have enough goods and wealth,
they will certainly head north.
Besides, the ice and snow have already melted,
and the situation makes it difficult for them to stay long,
we should wait for them to leave,
and then take it,
this can be ten thousand times secure."
Liú Zhīyuǎn's assessment was precise,
which is why when he raised troops and headed south,
the Khitan could not contend with him.
The Zhāoyì military commissioner Zhāng Cóng'ēn,
because his territory was close to Huái and Luò,
(Zhāoyì administered Lùzhōu.
From Lùzhōu to Zézhōu,
then to Huáizhōu to cross the river,
then Luòzhōu, Hénán prefecture.
Old Book of Táng, Treatise on Geography: From Lùzhōu to Luòzhōu is 470 lǐ.)
sent an envoy to consult with Zhīyuǎn,
Zhīyuǎn said:
"With my corner of land,
how dare I resist the vastness under heaven!
You should go first,
I will follow later."
Cóng'ēn thought this reasonable.
His判官 Gāo Fáng remonstrated:
"You are a close relative of the Jìn house,
(according to the Wǔdài Huìyào,
the former Empress Zhāng of the Jìn Shàodì,
was enfeoffed as empress in the eighth year of Tiānfú.
Zhāng Cóng'ēn was likely of the empress's clan.)
Cóng'ēn did not listen.
Left骁卫大将军 Wáng Shǒu'ēn,
was related by marriage to Cóng'ēn,
and was at that time in Shàngdǎng,
Cóng'ēn appointed his deputy Zhào Xíngqiān as acting留后,
(the deputy here,
is the deputy military commissioner.)
with Gāo Fáng assisting him.
Shǒu'ēn
was the son of Wáng Jiànlì.
Wáng Jiànlì served Táng Míngzōng and was trusted and employed,
and later served Jìn Gāozǔ.)
13 The Jīngnán military commissioner Gāo Cónghuì sent an envoy to present tribute to the Khitan,
and the Khitan sent an envoy to bestow horses upon him.
Cónghuì also sent an envoy to Hédōng to urge [Zhīyuǎn] to advance [to the throne].
The Gāo father and son of Jīngnán served the powerful to preserve their state,
their strategy was generally like this.
14 The Táng ruler established Prince Qí Jǐngsuì as皇太弟.
He transferred Prince Yān Jǐngdá to be Prince Qí,
and appointed him commander-in-chief of the various circuit armies;
transferred Prince Nánchāng Hóngjǐ to be Prince Yān,
as his deputy.
Jǐngsuì once held a banquet with his palace officials,
the赞善大夫 Zhāng Yì from Yuánchéng offered some规谏,
(Zhāng Yì was a northerner who served in Jiāngnán.)
but [Jǐngsuì] paid him no heed.
Yì angrily said:
"Your Highness values treasures and轻视 scholars."
He took a jade cup and threw it to the ground, shattering it;
everyone turned pale;
Jǐngsuì composed his expression and apologized to him,
and treated Yì even more generously.
Jǐngsuì's ability to reform and respect scholars
was also commendable.
Jǐngdá was by nature upright and blunt,
when the Táng ruler drank with his clan members and close ministers,
Féng Yánjǐ, Yánlǔ, Wèi Cén, Chén Jué and their ilk
displayed extreme fawning and flattering attitudes,
sometimes becoming喧笑 under the influence of wine;
Jǐngdá repeatedly rebuked and reprimanded them,
and also spoke bluntly to remonstrate with the Táng ruler,
that he should not be close to谄媚 ministers.
Yánjǐ, because the establishment of the two brothers was not his wish,
wanted to win them over with empty words;
once at a banquet in the Eastern Palace,
he pretended to be drunk,
patted Jǐngdá on the back and said:
"You must not forget me!"
Jǐngdá was greatly angered,
flicked his sleeves and entered the palace to report to the Táng ruler,
requesting to have him executed;
the Táng ruler explained and mediated,
and only then did he stop.
(At this time Chén Jué and Féng Yánlǔ were attacking Fúzhōu,
the history says they displayed extreme fawning and flattering attitudes while attending drinking sessions,
speaking generally of their usual behavior,
not necessarily confined to this time.)
"Petty men交构,
is a matter of fortune and misfortune.
Your Highness lacks the power to remove them,
yet repeatedly confronts them face to face,
making them fearful and prepared,
what might they not do!"
From then on, whenever there were excursions or banquets,
Jǐngdá often declined on grounds of illness and did not attend.
The Táng ruler sent an envoy to congratulate the Khitan on destroying Jìn,
and also requested to go to Cháng'ān to repair and restore
the various imperial tombs;
(at the end of the Táng, during the turmoil of collapse and disorder,
many of the imperial tombs were excavated;
Nán Táng claimed to继承 the Táng lineage,
hence the request to repair and restore them.)
and sent an envoy to report this.
The Jìn密州刺史 Huángfǔ Huī,
and Dìzhōu刺史 Wáng Jiàn,
both avoiding the Khitan,
led their followers and fled to Táng;
many of the rebel leaders north of the Huái requested orders from Táng.
The Táng虞部员外郎 Hán
Xīzǎi submitted a memorial,
believing that:
"Your Majesty is restoring the ancestral enterprise,
now is the time.
If the barbarian ruler returns north,
and the Central Plains has a ruler,
then it will not be easy to plan."
At that time they were engaged in war with Fúzhōu,
and had no leisure to look north;
the people of Táng all considered this a regret,
and the Táng ruler also regretted it.
Had Táng not had the Fúzhōu campaign,
and raised troops to head north,
it would only have resulted in the loss of armies.
The Khitan ruler summoned all the Jin officials to assemble in the courtyard,
and asked:
"My country is vast,
spanning tens of thousands of li,
with twenty-seven chieftains;

Ōuyáng Xiū said: According to Táng dynasty precedent: The Son of Heaven daily held court in the main hall to receive his ministers,
which was called "regular attendance."
On the first and fifteenth days of the month, when offerings were made at the imperial tombs,
the emperor, feeling a sense of longing and remembrance,
could not attend the front hall,
so he would receive his ministers in the side hall,
which was called "entering the inner chamber."
Xuānzhèng Hall was the front hall,
called the "public court,"
where guards were stationed.
Zǐchén Hall was the side hall,
called the "inner chamber."
When the emperor did not attend the front hall but instead went to Zǐchén Hall,
the guards were summoned from the main court to enter through the inner gate,
and the officials waiting for court at the main court
would follow them in to have an audience,
hence it was called "entering the inner chamber."
However, the main court was for formal court sessions,
and its rituals were dignified;
the inner chamber was for informal audiences,
and its proceedings were simplified.
After the Qiánfú era,
due to turmoil and the neglect of rituals,
the Son of Heaven could not see his ministers daily but only on the first and fifteenth days of the month,
so the guards at the main court were often dismissed on regular days,
while on the first and fifteenth days, when entering the inner chamber, guards were present.
Later, as this became customary,
"entering the inner chamber" came to be regarded as important,
to the extent that even when the emperor appeared in the front hall,
it was still called "entering the inner chamber."
During the Five Dynasties period,
ministers would have an audience once every five days in the Zhōngxīng Hall,
which was a side hall.
This was a remnant of the "entering the inner chamber" ritual,

On the first and fifteenth days of the month, the emperor would appear once in the Wénmíng Hall,
which was the front hall,

Now, according to the "Five Dynasties Compendium of Administrative Regulations," there is a ritual for "entering the inner chamber": The Directorate of Astronomy presents the time tablet,
the inner chamber gate presents the tablet indicating all officials are assembled,
the emperor, wearing a robe and boots from within the palace,
rides a palanquin to the gate of the regular audience hall and halts the palanquin,
receives the greetings of the Privy Councilor and below,
and is then escorted to the main audience hall.
After the emperor is seated,
the curtains are rolled up,
incense is added in the hall,
and a shout is given:
"The Imperial Guard officers bow."
Next, the cockcrow is announced,
then the inner chamber gate verifies the tally,
then the inner chamber gate official conveys the decree to summon the guards,
then the inner chamber gate envoy leads the Jīnyú general and the southern rank officials to bow, after which they are separately led to their positions and bow to each other,
then the minor guards enter in succession,
then the officials holding the civil and military registers proceed to their positions and bow to each other,
then the chief ministers and southern rank officials bow, after which they are separately led to their positions and bow to each other,
then the Jīnyú general reports:
"All is peaceful,"
then the civil and military officials enter.
The protocol officer bows in the hall,
enters the sandy courtyard in slippers,
bows twice and stands still,
then leads the chief ministers, officials from the two departments, and the Jīnyú general to stand together in formation,
the inner chamber gate envoy shouts:
"Bow,"
they insert their tablets, perform the dance,
bow three times,
and report:
"May Your Majesty enjoy boundless happiness";
then the chief minister at the head of the line is led forward,
bows twice again,
performs the dance,
kneels,
bows three times,
and is led back to his position to bow to the others.
The protocol officer leads the chief ministers to stand below the eastern and western stairways,
then the civil and military officials exit,
then the officials from the two departments bow in the hall and exit from the southern rank,
then the Hanlin academicians bow in the hall and exit from the southern rank,
then the officials holding the civil and military registers bow in the hall and exit from the southern rank,
then the Jīnyú general bows in the hall and exits from the southern rank,
then the minor guards exit;
then the chief ministers are led before the incense table to report matters, after which
the Xuānhuī envoy shouts:
"You may leave,"
and they bow in the hall and exit from the southern rank;
then the inner chamber gate envoy leads the waiting officials to their positions to bow twice,
leads them forward to report matters, after which
they return to their positions and bow deeply,
the Xuānhuī envoy announces:
"Your report is acknowledged,"
they bow twice again,
perform the dance,
kneel,
bow three times,
the protocol officer shouts:
"You may leave,"
and they bow in the hall and exit from the southern rank;
then the judicial officials report matters following the same procedure,
then the supervising censor bows in the hall and exits from the southern rank,
then the inner chamber gate official conveys the decree to dismiss the guards,
then the inner chamber gate envoy reports that there are no matters in the court,
then a shout is given:
"The Imperial Guard officers wait respectfully outside the gate,"
then the curtains are lowered,
and the emperor mounts the palanquin and returns to the inner palace.
Also, according to the "Historical Records of the Five Dynasties": On the first day of the ninth month of the first year of the Qiánhuà era of Liáng Tàizǔ (Xīnshì),
he held court in the Wénmíng Hall for the "entering the inner chamber" ritual.
Thus, the "entering the inner chamber" ritual was established by the Liáng dynasty.
Compared to the Táng dynasty's formal court assemblies,
its rituals were simplified and crude,
yet the Five Dynasties called it "performing the rituals."
The "Compendium of Administrative Regulations" also records it in detail and includes it in the book,
indicating that this ritual was considered the highest standard of its time.
I have recorded it here in full
to document the changes in court rituals.
Wénmíng Hall was the main audience hall of the Luòyáng Palace.
Chóngyuán Hall was the main audience hall of the Biàn Palace.

he will know that I have done nothing wrong.
If we now make further plans,
disaster will befall others,
the entire city will suffer,
what good will that ultimately do!"
The crowd still wanted to resist and hold out,
but the Commissioner of the Three Departments, Liú Shěnjiāo from Wén'ān, said:
"I am a man of Yān,
how could I not consider the Yān troops!
Wén'ān,
a Hàn dynasty county,
belonged to Mòzhōu in the Táng.
Speaking in terms of the major boundaries of the Warring States' seven powers,
then Yíng and Mò of the Táng
were both the southern borders of Yān;
speaking in terms of the Táng's regional military governors,
then Yíng and Mò
were under the jurisdiction of Lúlóng.
Therefore, Liú Shěnjiāo, whose family was from Wén'ān,
called himself a man of Yān.
Now, after the great chaos in the city,
both public and private resources are exhausted,
few survivors remain,
Biàn city had been plundered by Zhāng Yànzé,
and the Khitan swept everything northward,
hence this situation.
Jǐ,
pronounced as jū qǐ fān.
There will be no one left alive.
I hope you all say no more,
and fully comply with the Dowager's arrangements."
So they adopted the strategy of Zhào Yuǎn and Zhái Guāngyè,
proclaiming the title of Prince of Liáng,
overseeing military and state affairs.
Cóngyì's original title was Prince of Xǔ.
Because he was proclaimed in Dàliáng,
he called himself Prince of Liáng,
which meant he had already established a state and changed its name.
Now that they had submitted to welcome the Hàn,
why change the state name again!
This was the fault of the advisors at the time.
They requested to proceed to the capital early,
and then moved out to reside in a private residence.
On the Jiǎchén day,
the Emperor arrived at Jìnzhōu.
The Khitan ruler Wùyù, because the Khitan ruler Déguāng had a son in the country,
and he himself had succeeded as the nephew,
and also lacked the mandate of Empress Dowager Shùlǜ,
Empress Dowager Shùlǜ,
was Wùyù's grandmother.
Dǎn
inwardly felt uneasy.
Initially,
when the Khitan ruler Ābǎojī died in Bóhǎi,
Empress Dowager Shùlǜ killed chieftains and generals, numbering in the hundreds.
This event is recorded in the 275th scroll, second month of the first year of Tiānchéng era of Táng Míngzōng.
The chieftains and generals, fearing death,
then plotted to support the Khitan ruler Wùyù in leading troops back north.
The Khitan ruler appointed Má Dá, Military Governor of Ānguó, as留守 of Zhōngjīng,
the Old History of the Five Dynasties says: Má Dá,
was a cousin of Yēlǜ Déguāng;
his father was Sàlà.
During Ābǎojī's time,
he fled from the barbarian lands to Táng Zhuāngzōng,
then fled to Liáng.
When Zhuāngzōng pacified Liáng,
he captured him,
and had him torn apart by chariots in the market.
All the civil and military officials and soldiers of Jìn were left in Héngzhōu,
only taking with him Hanlin Academicians Xú Táifú, Lǐ Huàn, as well as palace women, eunuchs, and musicians.
Leaving the civil and military officials but taking palace women, eunuchs, and musicians with him,
the historian says this shows Wùyù lacked long-term vision.
On the Yǐsì day,
he departed from Zhēndìng.
Héngzhōu established Zhēndìng Prefecture.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
the Prefect of Jiàngzhōu, Lǐ Cónglǎng, and the Khitan general Chéng Bàqīng and others resisted the order.
Chéng,
is a surname.
The Hé family's surname registry: Originally descended from Chéng Bó, son of King Wén of Zhōu,
there was Duke Chéng Sù of Zhōu.
Also,
the Chǔ Prime Minister Zǐyù was enfeoffed at Chéng,
this was Chéng Déchén,
his descendants also took Chéng as their surname.
They had not yet surrendered.
The Hùguó Army was in Hézhōng Prefecture;
at that time, they had not yet obtained Hézhōng,
Bái Wénkē held the military governorship.
Kē,
pronounced as qiū hé fān.
He ordered the various armies to spread out and not attack,
and advised them on the advantages and disadvantages.
On the Wùshēn day,
Cónglǎng surrendered the entire city.
The Emperor ordered his trusted generals to separately guard the gates,
not allowing a single soldier to enter.
Fearing they would enter the city to plunder.
On the Xīnhài day,
the Emperor arrived at Shǎnzhōu,
Zhào Huī personally held the Emperor's horse and entered.
On the Rénzǐ day,
they arrived at Shíháo.
The Nine Regions Gazetteer: Shǎn County in Shǎnzhōu has Shíháo Town.
People from Biàn crossed Zhèng and Luò to come and welcome them,
showing how they suffered under the Khitan's oppressive rule,
and longed for the Hàn's arrival to bring relief,
but alas, in the end, it failed to meet their hopes!
On the fourteenth day of the sixth month,
the first day of the month being Jiǎyín,
Xiāo Hàn arrived at Héngzhōu
and, together with Má Dá, surrounded Zhāng Lì's residence with armored cavalry.
Lì was lying ill at the time.
He came out to meet them.
Hàn enumerated his faults, saying:
"Why did you tell the late emperor,
saying that Hú people cannot serve as military commissioners?
(Zhāng Lì's words
are recorded in the 285th scroll, in the third year of the Kāiyùn era of the Jìn Prince of Qí.)
(To enumerate
is pronounced as 'suǒ jù fān.')
I am the Xuānwǔ military commissioner,
and also a maternal uncle of the state;
yet you, in the Secretariat, dared to reprimand me!
Furthermore,
when the late emperor left me to guard Biànzhōu,
(see the third month of this year in the previous scroll.)
you considered it improper.
Also,
you slandered me and Xièlǐ before the late emperor,
saying Xièlǐ was fond of plundering people's wealth,
and I was fond of plundering people's sons and daughters.
Now I must kill you!"
He ordered him to be shackled.
Lì declared loudly:
"These were all matters concerning the fundamental principles of the state.
I indeed spoke of them.
If you wish to kill me, then kill me.
Why use shackles!"
Má Dá argued that a high minister should not be arbitrarily killed
and strenuously intervened to stop it.
Hàn then released him.
That evening,
Lì died of indignation and rage.
Cuī Tíngxūn went to see Má Dá.
He hurried forward and bowed,
rose,
knelt and offered wine.
Má Dá sat with his legs sprawled and received it.
(The historian remarks: Zhāng Lì was upright and defiant, so Xiāo Hàn did not dare kill him;
Cuī Tíngxūn was excessively obsequious, so Má Dá showed him no courtesy.)
On the fifteenth day, Yǐmǎo,
the Emperor arrived at Xīn'ān.
(Xīn'ān County belonged to the Hénán Prefecture of the Western Capital.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is seventy lǐ west of the capital.)
On the sixteenth day,
the Loyal and Wise King of Wúyuè, Qián Hóngzuǒ, died.
He was twenty years old.
On the seventeenth day, Bǐngchén,
the Emperor arrived at Luòyáng
and took up residence in the palace.
The officials of Biànzhōu sent memorials to welcome him.
An edict was issued to reassure those who had received appointments from the Qìdān, ordering them not to be suspicious,
and to gather and burn their letters of appointment.
Zhào Yuǎn changed his name to Shàngjiāo.
(To avoid the Emperor's personal name.)
(To change
is pronounced 'gōng héng fān.')
He ordered the Zhèngzhōu defense commissioner, Guō Cóngyì, to first enter Dàliáng to clear the palace,
secretly instructing him to kill Lǐ Cóngyì and Wáng Shū.
As Shū was about to die,
she said:
"My son was established by the Qìdān.
What crime has he committed to deserve death?
Why not spare him,
so that each year during the Cold Food Festival,
he could offer a bowl of wheat porridge and sprinkle libations at the tomb of Emperor Míngzōng?"
(The Wǔdài Huìyào states: The way for a ruler to honor his ancestors
does not include making offerings in the wild during the Cold Food Festival.
In recent times, Emperor Zhuāngzōng went out to make offerings every Cold Food Festival,
calling it 'pòsàn' (breaking up and scattering).
Thus, it was continued and practiced.
Ōuyáng Xiū said: Making offerings in the wild during Cold Food and burning paper money—
how long before China becomes no different from the barbarians!
According to a Táng Kāiyuán era decree:
'Making offerings at graves during Cold Food
is not mentioned in the classical rites.
In recent times, it has been passed down,
gradually becoming a custom.
It should be permitted to make offerings at graves as part of the worship and sweeping ritual.')
It seems the Táng permitted commoners and officials' families to practice this,
but rulers did not have this ritual.
As for the Hàn founder,
it would have been acceptable to spare Lǐ Cóngyì's life.
Killing him was excessive.)
On the eighteenth day, Wùwǔ,
the Emperor departed from Luòyáng.
The Bureau of Military Affairs clerk Wèi Rénpǔ escaped back from the Qìdān
and met him at Gǒng.
Guō Wēi asked him about troop numbers and past precedents.
Rénpǔ had a strong memory and was sharp and quick-witted.
Wēi thus became close to and trusted him.
(Rénpǔ
was from Wèizhōu.)
On the nineteenth day, Xīnyǒu,
the Biànzhōu officials, led by Dòu Zhèngù, welcomed him at Xíngyáng.
(Xíngyáng County belonged to Zhèngzhōu.
From Gǒng County east to Xíngyáng is one hundred and ninety lǐ.)
On the twenty-second day, Jiǎzǐ,
the Emperor arrived at Dàliáng.
The military governors of the former Jìn surrendered one after another.
On the twenty-fourth day, Bǐngyín,
the King of Wúyuè, Qián Hóngcóng, succeeded to the position.
On the twenty-sixth day, Wùchén,
the Emperor issued an edict granting a general amnesty.
All military commissioners appointed by the Qìdān,
down to the officers and officials,
were to remain in their posts,
with no further changes.
He also restored Biànzhōu as the Eastern Capital.
(The Qìdān had demoted the Eastern Capital to Biànzhōu;
see the first month of this year in the previous scroll.)
He still used the Tiānfú era name,
saying:
"I cannot bear to forget the Jìn."
He restored the three military commands of Qīng, Xiāng, and Rǔ.
(The Jìn likely abolished the Pínglú Army because of Yáng Guāngyuǎn's rebellion and the Shānnán East Circuit because of Ān Cóngjìn's rebellion.
Rǔzhōu had never been a military command;
it is probably Ānzhōu,
as the Ānyuǎn Army was abolished because of Lǐ Jīnquán's rebellion.)
However, after the Qìdān entered Biàn,
they had appointed Yáng Guāngyuǎn's son, Yáng Chéngxìn, as the Pínglú military commissioner.
It seems the Hàn, considering itself the successor to the Jìn,
abolished the Qìdān's policies,
not regarding them as established law.)
On the thirtieth day, Rénshēn,
he appointed the Běijīng留守 Liú Chóng as the military commissioner of Hédōng,
with the title of Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì.
The Qìdān Empress Dowager Shùlǜ heard that the Qìdān ruler had proclaimed himself emperor
and was greatly angered.
She dispatched troops to oppose him.
The Qìdān ruler sent Prince Wěi as the vanguard.
They met at the Stone Bridge.
(Hú Qiáo's Rù Liáo Lù states: Wùyù and Shùlǜ fought at the Shíqiáo on the Shā River.
This was likely the bridge over the Shā River.
To the south was Yáojiāzhōu,
to the north was Xuānhuàguǎn leading to Xīlóu.)
The former Jìn commander of the Imperial Guard Cavalry, Lǐ Yǎntāo, had followed the Jìn ruler northward.
(See the first month of this year in the previous scroll.)
The Empress Dowager appointed him as the deployment commander.
Yǎntāo surrendered to Prince Wěi.
The Empress Dowager's troops were thus greatly defeated.
The Qìdān ruler imprisoned the Empress Dowager at Ābǎojī's tomb.
(Hú Qiáo's Rù Liáo Lù states: Wùyù imprisoned Empress Shùlǜ at Pūmǎshān.
After traveling for another three days,
they finally reached Xīlóu.
The Ōu Shǐ states: The Qìdān established Zǔzhōu at Ābǎojī's tomb.
The Xiōngnú Xūzhī states: Zǔzhōu is fifty lǐ east of Shàngjīng;
Shàngjīng is Xīlóu.)
This is recorded here together.
As for the similarities and differences in place names,
and the distances in lǐ,
one must have personally traveled there to ascertain the accuracy.)
He proclaimed himself the Heaven-Appointed Emperor
and appointed Gāo Xūn as the Commissioner of Military Affairs.
The Qìdān ruler admired Chinese customs,
employing many former Jìn officials.
However, he indulged in wine and women,
and treated the various tribal chiefs with disrespect.
Consequently, the people did not support him,
and the various tribes rebelled frequently.
He raised troops to suppress them.
Thus, for several years,
he had no time to invade the south.
(The historian remarks: After China's period of turmoil and disorder,
it was able to gradually achieve some peace and stability because of this.)
Earlier,
the Qìdān ruler Déguāng had ordered the commander of the Fèngguó Capital Command, Nángōng Wáng Jìhóng,
(Nángōng County belonged to Jìzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is sixty-two lǐ southwest of the prefecture.)
and the Zhāngdé military commissioner Gāo Tángyīng to treat them well.
(Gāo Tángyīng
was appointed by the Qìdān;
see the fourth month of this year in the previous scroll.
(Xiàng
is pronounced 'xī liàng fān.')
Tángyīng supplied them with armor and weapons,
trusting them as if they were relatives.
When Tángyīng heard that the Emperor was moving south,
he requested to surrender the entire command.
Before the envoy returned,
Jìhóng and Huī killed Tángyīng.
Jìhóng declared himself acting military commissioner
and sent an envoy to report that Tángyīng was duplicitous.
An edict appointed Jìhóng as acting military commissioner of Zhāngdé.
On the twelfth day of the seventh month, Gēngchén,
Huī was appointed prefect of Cízhōu.
The Ānguó military commissioner Gāo Fèngmíng heard of Tángyīng's death
and felt uneasy.
He requested from Má Dá
to appoint the commander of the infantry and cavalry, Liú Duó, as deputy military commissioner,
to administer the military prefecture,
while he himself returned to Héngzhōu.
(Since Xíng and Xiàng could not be held,
how could Héngzhōu stand alone?
This sets the stage for the generals to expel Má Dá.)
The emperor dispatched an envoy to deliver a proclamation to Jīngnán.
Gāo Cónghuì submitted a memorial offering congratulations,
and also requested Yǐngzhōu,
but the emperor did not grant it.
When the envoy bearing additional imperial favors arrived,
Gāo Cónghuì refused to accept them.
Since the Táng dynasty,
when a new sovereign ascended the throne,
envoys were sent to bestow additional favors upon the various military governors.
Envoy,
shū lì fān.
25 The ruler of the Southern Táng, hearing that the Khitan ruler Dég uāng had died
and Xiāo Hàn had abandoned Dàliáng and departed,
issued an edict stating:
"We turn our gaze upon the Central Plains,
the former territory of our dynasty."
The Southern Táng ruler claimed descent from Prince Wú Kè,
hence he spoke thus.
Dynasty,
zhí yáo fān.
Jīnquán was appointed as the Northern Front Campaign Pacification Commissioner,
Lǐ Jīnquán,
a general of Jìn,
who had fled to the Southern Táng; see Volume 282, the fifth year of the Tiānfú era of Jìn Gāozǔ.
Hearing that the emperor had already entered Dàliáng,
he consequently did not dare to dispatch troops.
26 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the jiǎwǔ day,
Mǎ Xīguǎng was appointed as Generalissimo of the Tiāncè Army, Military Governor of Wǔ'ān, and Commander-in-Chief of the various circuits south of the Yangtze,
concurrently serving as Zhōngshū Lìng,
and enfeoffed as Prince of Chǔ.
Because of the additional favors bestowed upon his accession,
Mǎ Xīguǎng was consequently appointed with the official titles and ranks of his father and elder brother.
27 There were rumors that Zhào Yánshòu had died.
Guō Wēi said to the emperor:
"Zhào Kuāngzàn
was appointed by the Khitan,
see the first month of this year in the previous volume.
It is appropriate to send an envoy to offer condolences and sacrifices,
and on that occasion, to have him resume his duties and transfer him to another military governorship.
He now has neither family nor state to return to.
His father died among the captors,
so he has no family to return to;
the Khitan have gone north,
so he has no state to return to."
The emperor followed this advice.

It happened that Dù Chóngwēi, the Liúshǒu of Yèdū and Military Governor of Tiānxióng concurrently serving as Zhōngshū Lìng, and Lǐ Shǒuzhēn, Military Governor of Tiānpíng concurrently serving as Shìzhōng, both submitted memorials pledging allegiance.
Chóngwēi further requested to be transferred to another military governorship.
Gāo Xíngzhōu, Military Governor of Guīdé concurrently serving as Zhōngshū Lìng, came to court.
On the bǐngshēn day,
Chóngwēi was transferred to be Military Governor of Guīdé,
and Xíngzhōu replaced him;
Dù Chóngwēi soon refused to hand over his command,
so Gāo Xíngzhōu was ordered to attack him.
He was additionally appointed concurrently as Zhōngshū Lìng;
this sets the stage for Lǐ Shǒuzhēn's occupation of Hézhōng.
Two years later,
Yánshòu finally died among the Khitan.
The history clarifies the falseness of the rumor.
28 The King of Wúyuè, Qián Hóngcóng, appointed his younger brother, Táizhōu Cìshǐ Qián Hóngchù, to jointly participate in the affairs of the ministerial administration.
29 Lǐ Dá appointed his younger brother Tōng as Liúshǒu of Fúzhōu.
Lǐ Réndá had surrendered to the Southern Táng,
and the Southern Táng bestowed upon him the name Hóngyì,
enrolling him in the imperial clan register.
When he rebelled against the Southern Táng
and was attacked by them,
he sought aid from Wúyuè.
Since the character "Hóng" violated a Wúyuè taboo,
he changed his name to Dá.
His younger brother was originally named Hóngtōng,
and was also simply named Tōng.
Hóngcóng, acting under imperial authority, additionally appointed Dá as concurrent Shìzhōng,
and changed his name to Rúyūn.
Soon after, Rúyūn regretted and feared,
regretting his coming,
and fearing death.
He requested to return to Fúzhōu;
Jìn Sī interceded on his behalf,
and Hóngcóng agreed.
30 Dù Chóngwēi, considering that he had attached himself to the Khitan
and betrayed the Central Kingdom,
see the events in Volume 285, the third year of the Kāiyùn era of Jìn Qíwáng.
When the edict for his transfer arrived,
he again refused to accept it,
and sent his son Hóngsuì as a hostage to Má Dá to seek aid.
Zhào Yánshòu had two thousand personal troops from Yōuzhōu stationed in Héngzhōu.
Zhào Yánshòu was taken north in chains by the Khitan ruler Wù Yù,
and his personal troops remained in Héngzhōu.
Héng,
hù dēng fān.
Chóngwēi requested to use them to defend Wèi;
this sets the stage for Zhāng Liǎn assisting Dù Chóngwēi in holding firm.
General,
jí liàng fān.
In the intercalary month,
on the gēngwǔ day,
an edict was issued stripping Chóngwēi of his offices and ranks,
appointing Gāo Xíngzhōu as Campaign Pacification Commissioner,
with Mùróng Yǎnchāo, Military Governor of Zhènníng, as his deputy,
to campaign against Chóngwēi.
This sets the stage for Mùróng Yǎnchāo relying on his influence to bully Gāo Xíngzhōu, leading to discord among the commanders.
31 On the xīnwèi day,
Yáng Bīn, Guō Wēi, and Wáng Zhāng were all made full commissioners.
When the emperor ascended the throne in Tàiyuán,
he appointed Yáng Bīn as acting Shūmìshǐ,
Guō Wēi as acting Deputy Shūmìshǐ,
and Wáng Zhāng as acting Sānsīshǐ.
Now they were all made full commissioners.
Public and private resources were exhausted,
but when the troops who came from the north joined with the court's troops,
their numbers suddenly increased severalfold.
The troops from the north
refer to those who followed the emperor and Shǐ Hóngzhào from Tàiyuán.
The court's troops
refer to the old troops of the Jìn dynasty.
By eliminating wasteful expenditures to support the army,
the expenses were adequately covered.
32 On the gēngchén day,
an edict was issued to establish the imperial ancestral temple.
Tàizǔ Gāo Huángdì
and Shìzǔ Guāngwǔ Huángdì
were both to remain in perpetuity without being moved.
Furthermore, four temples for close ancestors were established,
and posthumous titles were conferred.
The Wǔdài Huìyào records: Posthumously honoring great-grandfather Tuān as Míngyuán Huángdì,
temple name Wénzǔ;
great-great-grandfather Áng as Gōngxī Huángdì,
temple name Dézǔ;
grandfather Zhuàn as Zhāoxiàn Huángdì,
temple name Yìzǔ;
father Tiǎn as Zhāngshèng Huángdì,
temple name Xiǎnzǔ.
33 Má Dá was greedy, cunning, cruel, and ruthless.
If commoners possessed precious goods or beautiful women,
he would certainly seize them.
He also arrested villagers,
falsely accusing them of being bandits.
He would peel their faces,
gouge out their eyes,
sever their wrists,
burn and roast them to death,
wishing to intimidate the masses.
He often carried the tools for these acts with him.
Tools,
referring to the implements for peeling faces, gouging eyes, severing wrists, and burning.
He would hang human livers, gallbladders, hands, and feet,
and eat, drink, live, and rest among them,
talking and laughing as usual.
When going out or coming in, he sometimes wore yellow robes,
used the imperial carriage,
and employed imperial regalia,
saying:
"These matters are considered impermissible by the Hàn people,
but in our country there are no such taboos."
Also, because the number of chancellors was insufficient,
he issued a directive ordering Féng Dào to oversee the Hóngwén Guǎn,
Lǐ Sōng to oversee the Shǐ Guǎn,
Hé Níng to oversee the Jíxián Yuàn,
and Liú Xù to oversee the Zhōngshū Shěng.
His presumption and audacity were such as this.
For chancellors to separately oversee
requires the issuance of an imperial edict,
yet Má Dá implemented it by directive.
The history records his presumption and audacity.
He showed no leniency or pardon,
therefore the markets and shops were not disturbed.
He constantly feared that Hàn people might recklessly
leave,
and said to the gatekeepers:
"If any Hàn person is seen peeping at the gate,
immediately cut off his head and bring it here."
Má Dá dispatched an envoy to supervise transportation in Míngzhōu.
The Míngzhōu Defense Commissioner Xuē Huáiràng, hearing that the emperor had entered Dàliáng,
killed his envoy
and surrendered the entire prefecture.
The emperor dispatched Guō Cóngyì with ten thousand troops to join Huáiràng in attacking Liú Duó in Xíngzhōu,
but they did not succeed.
Liú Duó was holding Xíngzhōu for the Khitan.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Míngzhōu is ninety lǐ northwest to Xíngzhōu.
Má Dá dispatched his general Yáng Ān and the former Military Governor of Yìwǔ, Lǐ Yīn, with a thousand cavalry to attack Huáiràng in Míngzhōu.
Huáiràng defended the city walls and held out,
while Ān and others unleashed their troops to plage extensively in the territories of Xíngzhōu and Míngzhōu.
The Khitan troops left behind numbered less than two thousand,
referring to the troops left in Héngzhōu.
They gathered the rest to take for themselves.
Mádá often suspected the Hàn troops,
and considered them useless,
gradually dismissing and reducing them,
while cutting their rations to feed the Hú soldiers;
the hearts of the masses were filled with resentment and anger,
and upon hearing that the Emperor had entered Dàliáng,
they all harbored the desire to return south.
The former Yǐngzhōu Defense Commissioner Hé Fújìn,
the Kòng Hè Commandant Tàiyuán Lǐ Róng,
secretly gathered several dozen strong men from the army to plot an attack against the Khitan,
but they feared that the Khitan were still strong,
and hesitated to act.
It happened that Yáng Gǔn, Yáng Ān, and others led their troops out,
with Yáng Gǔn heading to Wèizhōu,
and Yáng Ān attacking Míngzhōu.
Hé Fújìn and the others then decided on their plan,
agreeing to strike the Buddhist temple bell as the signal.
They agreed that when the Hàn troops heard the Buddhist temple bell struck,
they would all emerge together to attack the Khitan.
However, the Buddhist temple strikes the bell at dawn and dusk,
and at mealtime,
every day;
this must have been prearranged before the action,
so that upon hearing the Buddhist temple bell at mealtime the next day, they would all act together.
On the Xīnsì day,
the Khitan ruler Wùyù sent cavalry to Héngzhōu,
summoning the former Wēishèng Military Commissioner and concurrently Zhōngshū Lìng Féng Dào, Privy Councilor Lǐ Sōng, Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs Hé Níng, and others,
to attend the burial of the Khitan ruler Déguāng at Mùyè Shān.
Féng Dào and the others had not yet departed,
when at mealtime,
the bell sounded.
The Hàn troops seized the weapons of the Khitan guards at the gate and attacked the Khitan,
killing over ten people,
and then rushed into the government compound.
Lǐ Róng first occupied the armory,
summoned all the Hàn troops and townspeople,

This sets the stage for the later execution of Dù Chóngwēi and the people of the market eating his flesh.
The character "诟" (curse) is pronounced "kòu",
and also "hòu".
Your subject Guāng comments: Hàn Gāozǔ's killing of 1,500 innocent people from Yōuzhōu
was not benevolent;
luring Zhāng Liǎn and then executing him
was not trustworthy;
pardoning Dù Chóngwēi despite his great crimes
was not just.
Benevolence is used to unite the masses,
trustworthiness to enforce orders,
and justice to punish evildoers.
Losing these three,
how can one preserve the state!
It is fitting that his dynasty's fortune did not last long!
49. Gāo Xíngzhōu, because Mùróng Yànchāo was at Chánzhōu,
firmly declined the post at Yèdū;
Chán and Wèi are separated by one hundred and fifty li.
Xíngzhōu and Yànchāo were already on bad terms,
residing in adjacent territories,
they would certainly not coexist peacefully,
hence he firmly declined.
On the jǐmǎo day,
Shǐ Hóngzhào, Military Commissioner of Zhōngwǔ, was appointed to concurrently hold the post of Military Commissioner of Guīdé,
and also Commander of the Imperial Guard Cavalry and Infantry;
Liú Xìn, Military Commissioner of Yìchéng, was appointed to concurrently hold the post of Military Commissioner of Zhōngwǔ and Deputy Commander of the Imperial Guard Cavalry and Infantry;
Yànchāo was transferred to become Military Commissioner of Tiānpíng,
and all were additionally appointed as Tóng Píngzhāng Shì.
50. The King of Wúyuè, Qián Hóngzòng, conducted a grand review of the navy,
with rewards and gifts doubled compared to before;
Hú Jìnsī firmly remonstrated,
Hóngzòng became angry,
threw his writing brush into the water,
and said:
"My wealth is shared with the soldiers,
why should there be a limit on how much or how little!"
This laid the groundwork for Hú Jìnsī's later deposition of Hóngzòng.
51. In the twelfth month,
on the bǐngxū day,
the Emperor departed from Yèdū.
He set out from Yèdū and returned to Dàliáng.
52. The ruler of Shǔ dispatched Wú Chóngyùn, the Yāyá of the Xióngwǔ Army,
(Yāyá of the Xióngwǔ Army
is the Yāyá of Qínzhōu).
Yùn,
is pronounced yùn.
On the gēngyín day,
Zhāng Qiánzhāo, Military Commissioner of Shānnán Xīdào and concurrently Zhōngshū Lìng, was appointed as the Pacification Commissioner of the Northern Front Campaign,
with Hé Chóngjiàn, Military Commissioner of Xióngwǔ, as his deputy;
(Zhāng Qiánzhāo, during the rebellion of the Prince of Lù,
attacked Fèngxiáng and was defeated,
then surrendered to Shǔ.
Hé Chóngjiàn surrendered to Shǔ when the Khitan entered the Central Plains,
hence the ruler of Shǔ employed them to manage Qí and Yōng).
Chóng,
is pronounced zhí.
Together they led fifty thousand troops,
Qiánzhāo marched out through Sànguān,
Chóngjiàn marched out through Lǒngzhōu,
to attack Fèngxiáng;
having already sent an envoy to summon Hóu Yì,
they followed it up with troops to threaten him.
To aid Cháng'ān.
This was in response to Zhào Kuāngzàn's request.
Their banners and flags stretched for several tens of li.
53. On the xīnmǎo day,
the Emperor's son, Chéngxùn, the Prefect of Kāifēng, passed away.
Chéngxùn was filial, friendly, loyal, and honest,
skilled in governance,
and everyone lamented his loss.
History records that with Chéngxùn's death, the fortunes of the Hàn dynasty declined.
54. On the guǐsì day,
the Emperor arrived at Dàliáng.
55. Lǐ Rúyūn, Military Commissioner of Wēiwǔ, was at odds with Bào Xiūràng, the Wúyuè garrison commander,
and plotted to ambush and kill Xiūràng,
intending to surrender Fúzhōu to Táng again;
Xiūràng discovered the plot,
led troops to attack the official residence,
and on that day,
killed Rúyūn,
exterminating his clan.
(Lǐ Réndá's occupation of Fúzhōu was first recorded in the second year of the Kāiyùn era of the Qí Prince of Jìn, in volume 285).
History shows that those who are treacherous and duplicitous ultimately die at the hands of others.
56. On the yǐwèi day,
the posthumous title of Prince of Wèi was conferred upon the Emperor's son Chéngxùn.
57. Hóu Yì requested to surrender to Shǔ,
and sent Wú Chóngyùn to take the military registers and grain accounts back west,
submitting a joint memorial with Zhào Kuāngzàn requesting to send troops to pacify Guānzhōng.
58. On the jǐyǒu day,
Bào Xiūràng sent the head of Lǐ Rúyūn to Qiántáng,
and the King of Wúyuè, Qián Hóngzòng, appointed Wú Chéng of Shānyīn, the Chancellor, to administer the affairs of the Military Commissioner of Wēiwǔ.
59. The King of Wúyuè, Qián Hóngzòng,
was by nature stern and severe,
resenting that during the time of the loyal and devoted King Qián Hóngzuǒ, the generals were indulged and nurtured,
and policies did not originate from himself.
(According to the Old History of the Five Dynasties: When the King of Wúyuè, Qián Liú, faced the rebellion of Xú Wǎn,
he sent his son Yuánguàn as a hostage to Xuānzhōu,
taking Hú Jìnsī, Dài Yùn, and others with him.
Yuánguàn succeeded to the throne,
and appointed Jìnsī as a senior general.
After Yuánguàn's death, Hóngzuǒ succeeded,
and Jìnsī, considering himself an old general,
was highly respected and honored.
When Hóngzòng succeeded,
he treated Jìnsī with considerable contempt and disrespect,
which Jìnsī could not bear).
He executed three law-breaking officials from Háng and Yuè.
("Wǔ"
should be
"wǔ" [meaning to manipulate]).
Hú Jìnsī, Commander of the Inner Guard, relying on his merit in supporting Hóngzòng's accession,
interfered in government affairs;
Hóngzòng detested this,
and wanted to appoint him to a prefecture,
intending to strip him of his military authority and send him away.
Whenever Jìnsī proposed plans or opinions,
Hóngzòng often refuted him to his face.
Jìnsī returned home,
set up a memorial tablet for the loyal and devoted King (Hóngzuǒ),
loosened his hair, and wailed bitterly.
Shù,
is pronounced suǒ.
Zhé,
is pronounced zhī.
Pī,
is pronounced pí.
An official investigated him,
and reported that he had purchased nearly a thousand jin of meat.
Hóngzòng asked Jìnsī:
"How much meat does a large ox yield?"
He replied:
"No more than three hundred jin."
Hóngzòng said:
"Then the official's report is false."
And ordered the official's crime to be investigated.
Jìnsī bowed and praised his discernment.
Hóngzòng said:
"How do you know the details so well?"
Jìnsī, flustered, replied:
"Before I joined the army,
I was also engaged in this trade."
Jìnsī believed Hóngzòng knew about his humble origins,
and was deliberately shaming him,
increasing his resentment and anger.
(This is why Chǔ Suìliáng warned Táng Tàizōng not to press Zhāng Xuánsù too hard).
See above, seventh month.
(Meaning he again wanted to surrender to Táng).
Jìnsī grew increasingly uneasy.
Hóngzòng plotted with Hé Chéngxùn, Commander of the Inner Guard, to expel Jìnsī,
and also consulted Shuǐqiū Zhāoquàn, the Chief Supervisor of the Inner Palace.
(According to the Old History of the Five Dynasties: The mother of Qián Liú, King of Wúyuè, was from the Shuǐqiū clan,
so Zhāoquàn was likely a maternal relative).
(He advised) it would be better to tolerate him,
but Hóngzòng hesitated and could not decide.
Chéngxùn, fearing the plot would be exposed,
instead informed Jìnsī of the plan.
As the ancients said,
"Hesitation is the thief of success."
Hóngzòng's hesitation and indecision
caused Hé Chéngxùn to fear and change his mind.
Xiè,
is pronounced xiè.
On the last day of the month, gēngxū,
Hóngzòng held a night banquet for his generals and officials,
Jìnsī suspected he was plotting against him,
and conspired with his partisans to stage a rebellion.
Leading a hundred personal soldiers
in military attire and armed, he entered to see Hóngzòng in the Tiāncè Hall,
saying:
"This old slave is without fault,
why does Your Majesty plot against me?"
Hóngzòng shouted at him to withdraw, but he did not retreat,
and the armed attendants on both sides were filled with indignation.
Hóngzòng, taken by surprise and stunned, had no time to speak.
(If he had) utilized the indignation of his attendants,
and acted in the name of righteousness against rebellion,
what would he have to fear from Hú Jìnsī!
This shows the importance of a person having courage and decisiveness.
Jìnsī locked the doors,
falsely proclaimed the king's order,
and announced to the court and outside:
"(The king) suddenly fell ill with a wind-stroke,
and transmits the throne to Qián Hóngchù, who participates in the affairs of the Chancellor's office."
Jìnsī then led the generals to welcome Hóngchù from his private residence,
and summoned the Chancellor Yuán Dézhāo.
When Dézhāo arrived,
he stood outside the curtain and did not bow,
saying:
"I will wait to see the new ruler."
Jìnsī hurried out and lifted the curtain,
and only then did Dézhāo bow.
Jìnsī, claiming Hóngzòng's order,
acting under imperial authority, appointed Hóngchù as Military Commissioner of Zhènhǎi and Zhèndōng, concurrently Zhōngshù Lìng.
Hóngchù said:
"Only if my elder brother's life can be spared,
dare I accept this command.
Otherwise,
I should yield to a worthier path."
Jìnsī agreed.
Hóngchù then began to handle affairs.
Jìnsī killed Shuǐqiū Zhāoquàn and Jìnshì Lù Guāngxuàn.
(Jìnshì
is an official position established by Wúyuè to serve by the king's side).
(Zhāoquàn was Hóngzòng's maternal uncle).
Jìnsī's wife said:
"Others may be killed;
but Zhāoquàn
is a gentleman,
how can you harm him!"
History shows that sometimes women possess wisdom and insight surpassing that of men.
In this year,
the Tang ruler appointed the Grand General of the Yǔlín Guards, Wáng Yánzhèng, as the Prince of Póyáng and Military Commissioner of Ānhuà,
to garrison Ráozhōu.
The Tang had established the Ānhuà Army in Ráozhōu.
Wáng Yánzhèng's surrender to the Tang is recorded in the 284th scroll, in the second year of the Kāiyùn era of the Jìn Prince of Qí,
which corresponds to the third year of the Bǎodà era of the Southern Táng.
First year of the Qiányòu era (Wùshēn, 948)
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the Yǐmǎo day,
a general amnesty was declared,
and the era name was changed.
2 The Emperor, because Zhào Kuàngzàn and Hóu Yì were jointly causing trouble with the Shǔ army,
was troubled by this.
It happened that the Uighurs came to offer tribute,
complaining that they were being obstructed by the Dǎngxiàng,
and that since the Chángxīng era of the Táng,
the Dǎngxiàng tribes along the western route had been plundering envoys and tribute from foreign lands.
Although the Táng had dispatched troops to campaign against them,
they were unable to stop them.
Dǎng,
pronounced dǐlǎng fān.
An edict ordered the Grand General of the Left Guard, Wáng Jǐngchóng, and General Qí Cángzhēn to lead several thousand imperial guards to go there,
thereby having them manage affairs west of the passes.
Using the pretext of receiving the Uighur envoys to dispatch troops,
the real purpose was to manage affairs in the region west of the passes.
The administrative assistant of the Jìnchāng military governor, Lǐ Shù,
had long served under Zhào Yánshòu,
and Yánshòu sent him to assist Kuàngzàn.
When Kuàngzàn was about to go to Shǔ,
Shù remonstrated, saying:
"Did the Prince of Yàn enter the court
willingly?
This refers to Zhào Yánshòu being taken captive by the Khitan and going north.
Now is the time to focus on summoning and pacifying.
If you confess your crimes and return to court,
you will surely preserve your wealth and honor.
Going to Shǔ is not a sound plan.
'A hoof-print puddle cannot hold a foot-long carp.'
Words of Liú Yào.
Cén,
pronounced chúzhēn fān.
Tíchén,
refers to the water that collects in the footprints left by cattle and horses,
forming a stagnant pool,
not a place where a carp over a foot long can find room;
this metaphorically describes Shǔ as a small state,
whose situation cannot accommodate Zhào Kuàngzàn.
Kuàngzàn then sent Shù to present a memorial requesting to enter the court.
Jǐngchóng and the others had not yet departed when Shù arrived.
The Emperor asked Shù:
"Why did Kuàngzàn attach himself to Shǔ?"
He replied:
"Kuàngzàn felt that he himself held office under the barbarians,
referring to his earlier appointment by the Khitan ruler Yēlǜ Déguāng to garrison Hézhōng Prefecture.
His father,
meaning Zhào Yánshòu.
Therefore he attached himself to Shǔ seeking a temporary reprieve.
I believed that the state would certainly offer protection and pacification,
so he sent me to come and plead for mercy."
The Emperor said:
"Kuàngzàn and his father,
were originally our people,
unfortunately they fell among the barbarians.
Now Yánshòu has just fallen into a pit trap,
Zhào Yánshòu was imprisoned by the Khitan,
the event is recorded in the fifth month of last year.
I will permit him to enter the court.
Hóu Yì also requested to attend the celebration of the Sacred Birthday Festival on the fourth day of the second month.
The Wǔdài Huìyào records: The Emperor was born on the fourth day of the second month in the second year of the Qiánníng era of the Táng.
The Emperor summoned him into his private chambers,
and instructed him, saying:
"The intentions of Kuàngzàn and Yì
are both unknown.
When you arrive there,
if they have already entered the court,
then do not question them;
if they still delay and look around hesitantly,
you should act according to circumstances as you see fit."
3 On the Jǐwèi day,
the Emperor changed his name to Hào.
4 The former Military Commissioner of Wēishèng, Féng Dào, was appointed Grand Preceptor.
5 On the Rénxū day,
the King of Wúyuè, Qián Hóngchù, moved the former king, Qián Hóngzōng, to the private residence at the Yìjǐn Army,
moved to the private residence in Lín'ān.
He secretly warned him, saying:
"If there are any unusual measures taken against you,
they are not my intention,
you should resist them unto death."
6 Since the death of the Prince of Wèi, Liú Chéngxùn,
the Emperor had been excessively grief-stricken.
On the Jiǎzǐ day,
he first became unwell.
7 Zhào Kuàngzàn did not wait for Lǐ Shù to return with a reply,
and had already left Cháng'ān.
On the Bǐngzǐ day,
he entered for an audience.
When Wáng Jǐngchóng and the others reached Cháng'ān,
they heard that the Shǔ troops had already entered the Qínchuān region,
from north of the Dàsǎn Pass reaching to Qí and Yōng,
flanking both the north and south banks of the Wèi River,
a thousand li of fertile plains,
called Qínchuān.
They mobilized the troops of their own circuit and over a thousand of Zhào Kuàngzàn's personal guards to jointly resist them.
Their own circuit,
refers to the Jìnchāng circuit.
They wanted to tattoo their faces,
subtly revealing the intention;
the military officer Zhào Sīwǎn,
was the first to request to tattoo his own face to lead his subordinates,
tattooing their faces with the army designation,
so that if they fled, they would have nowhere to go.
Xiào,
pronounced hùjiào fān.
Shuài,
read as lǜ.
Qí Cángzhēn said privately:
"Sīwǎn is fierce and violent, difficult to control,
it would be better to kill him."
Jǐngchóng did not listen.
Sīwǎn
was from Wèizhōu.
This sets the stage for Zhào Sīwǎn's later occupation of Cháng'ān in rebellion.
When Shǔ's Lǐ Tíngguī was about to reach Cháng'ān,
he heard that Zhào Kuàngzàn had already entered the court,
and wanted to lead his troops back.
Wáng Jǐngchóng intercepted him,
and defeated Tíngguī at Zǐwǔ Valley.
Zhāng Qiánzhāo reached Bǎojī,
but the various generals' deliberations were not in harmony,
and they halted their troops without advancing;
Hóu Yì, hearing that Tíngguī had turned back west,
thereupon closed his fortifications and resisted the Shǔ troops.
Qiánzhāo's situation became isolated,
and he led his troops away in a night retreat.
Jǐngchóng led the troops of Fèngxiáng, Lǒng, Bīn, Jīng, Fū, and Fāng to pursue and defeat the Shǔ troops at the Sǎn Pass,
capturing over four hundred officers and soldiers.
The armies of Lǐ Tíngguī and Zhāng Qiánzhāo
were both dispatched by the Shǔ ruler in the twelfth month of last year.
Shuài,
read as lǜ.
Fū,
pronounced fū.
Bà,
pronounced bǔmài fān.
8 On the Dīngchǒu day,
the Emperor's condition became critical.
Yáng Bīn was suspicious of the Commander of the Imperial Guard Cavalry, Military Commissioner of Zhōngwǔ, Liú Xìn,
and immediately sent him to his garrison.
Liú Xìn, being a cousin, was in charge of the imperial guards,
therefore Yáng Bīn was suspicious of him,
and sent him to his garrison at Xǔzhōu.
He left weeping profusely.
Weeping so that tears fell like rain,
is called yǔqì.
The Emperor summoned Sū Féngjí, Yáng Bīn, Shǐ Hóngzhào, and Guō Wēi to receive his final instructions,
saying:
"My breath is faint,
I cannot speak much.
Chéngyòu is young and weak,
I entrust future affairs to you gentlemen."
He also said:
"Be careful to guard against Zhòngwēi."
This instructed them to execute Dù Zhòngwēi.
He passed away in the Wànsuì Hall,
at the age of fifty-four.
The Old History of the Five Dynasties records: When the Liáng received the abdication,
they renamed the Dàliáng Wànsuì Hall as the Wànsuì Hall.
On the Gēngchén day,
an edict was issued,
stating:
"Zhòngwēi and his sons,
taking advantage of my minor illness,
spread slanderous talk to stir up the masses.
Together with his sons Hóngzhāng, Hóngliǎn, and Hóngcàn, they are all to be executed."
The Jìn princess and all internal and external relatives,
are not to be questioned in any way."
The Jìn princess,
surnamed Shí,
was Dù Zhòngwēi's wife.
The people of the market vied to eat his flesh,
the officials could not stop them,
and it was completely consumed in a short while.
In the second month,
on the Xīnsì day, the first day of the month,
the Emperor's son, the Grand General of the Left Guard and Grand Palace Inspector, Liú Chéngyòu, was established as the Prince of Zhōu,
and given the title of Tóngpíngzhāngshì.
After a short while,
the funeral was held,
the will was proclaimed,
ordering the Prince of Zhōu to ascend the imperial throne.
He was eighteen years old at the time.
9. Shǔ generals Hán Bǎozhēn and Páng Fúchéng led their troops back from Lǒngzhōu,
Hán Bǎozhēn had also been dispatched by the Shǔ ruler in the twelfth month of the previous year.
They returned,
the pronunciation of 'cóng' follows the 'Xuān' reading,
and also the usual reading.
On that day,
Bǎozhēn and others reached Qínzhōu,
divided their troops to guard the various gates and main roads,
and Chóng Jiàn subsequently entered Shǔ.
10. On Dīnghài,
the Empress was honored as Empress Dowager.
11. The court knew that the Chéngdé acting military commissioner Bái Zàiróng was not a talented commander,
on Gēngyín,
he was replaced by the former Jiànxióng acting military commissioner Liú Zàimíng.
11. On Guǐsì,
a general amnesty was declared.
An amnesty was granted thirteen days after the emperor's accession.
13. Wúyuè's Inner Guards Commander Hé Chéngxùn again requested the execution of Hú Jìnsī and his faction.
The King of Wúyuè, Qián Hóngchù, disliked his fickleness,
and also feared it would invite disaster,
on Yǐwèi,
he arrested Chéngxùn,
and executed him.
Jìnsī repeatedly requested the killing of the deposed king Qián Hóngzōng to eliminate future troubles,
but Hóngchù refused.
Jìnsī then fraudulently issued a royal order secretly instructing Xuē Wēn to harm him,
Wēn said:
"On the day I received the command,
I did not hear these words,
I dare not act recklessly."
Jìnsī then sent two of his partisans, Fāng Ān and another, over the wall at night,
Hóngzōng barricaded the door and resisted them,
shouting loudly for help;
Wēn heard this,
led his men inside,
and killed Ān and the other in the courtyard.
He entered and reported to Hóngchù,
who had come from Lín'ān to Qiántáng to report the matter.
He said:
"That my elder brother is safe,
is due to your efforts."
Hóngchù feared and was wary of Jìnsī,
and humored him with feigned compliance.
Jìnsī was also inwardly anxious and fearful,
before long,
a carbuncle erupted on his back and he died.
Hóngzōng was thus preserved.
14. An edict appointed Wáng Jǐngchóng concurrently as Fèngxiáng Patrol and Inspection Commissioner.
Jǐngchóng led troops to Fèngxiáng,
Hóu Yì had not yet departed,
Jǐngchóng used imperial guards to garrison the various gates.
Someone advised Jǐngchóng to kill Yì,
but Jǐngchóng, having received a secret decree from the previous emperor,
(the secret decree,
refers to the command from Gāozǔ's bedside to act according to circumstances,
see above.)
cháo,
pronounced zhí yáo fān;
same below.
and fearing suspicion of unauthorized killing,
hesitated and could not decide.
Yì heard of this,
left without informing Jǐngchóng,
Jǐngchóng regretted it,
and cursed himself.
On Wùxū,
Yì entered the court,
the Hidden Emperor asked:
"Why did you summon Shǔ troops?"
He replied:
"Your subject intended to lure them in and kill them."
The Emperor smiled derisively.
15. Shǔ general Zhāng Qiánzhāo resented his lack of achievement,
on Guǐmǎo,
he reached Xīngzhōu,
and died of shame and anger.
He had returned from Sànguān to Xīngzhōu.
Zhāng Qiánzhāo was evidently a man who did not know what was feasible,
did not assess advantages and disadvantages,
and was overly eager for merit,
as seen in his attacks on Wáng Dū at Dìngzhōu,
and on the Prince of Lù at Fèngxiáng,
both cases of being overly eager for victory leading to defeat, as is already known.
huì,
pronounced yú bì fān.
16. The Commander of the Imperial Guard Cavalry and Infantry and Tongpingzhangshi Shǐ Hóngzhào suffered the loss of his mother,
within a few days,
he resumed attending court audiences.

Later Scholar from Tiāntái
First year of Qiányòu (Wùshēn, 948)
1. In the third month,
on Bǐngchén,
Shǐ Hóngzhào was recalled from mourning,
and additionally appointed concurrent Zhōngshū Lìng.
2. Hóu Yì's family was wealthy,
he heavily bribed the chief ministers and Shǐ Hóngzhào and others,
as a result, the high officials competed in praising him.
The chief ministers,
refers to Sū Féngjí, Yáng Bīn and others,
all were high officials at the time.
yù,
pronounced yú.
On Bǐngyín,
Yì was appointed concurrent Zhōngshū Lìng,
and acting Kāifēng Prefect.
'Acting' means,
performing the duties of Prefect,
not formally appointed.
3. Guǎngjìn
was changed to Dàmíng Prefecture,
Zuǒzhuàn: Jìn diviner Bǔ Yǎn said:
"Wèi,
is a great name."
This was taken to name the prefecture.
To abolish the Jìn mandate,
therefore Guǎngjìn and Jìnchāng were changed.
4. Hóu Yì severely slandered Wáng Jǐngchóng at court,
saying he was arrogant and tyrannical.
Hóu Yì, because Wáng Jǐngchóng had wanted to kill him,
fortunately escaped and returned to court,
therefore slandered him.
hèng,
pronounced hù mèng fān.
Jǐngchóng, knowing the situation had changed,
was inwardly uneasy,
and moreover resented the court.
He resented that the court could not understand the late emperor's intended purpose,
but instead listened to Hóu Yì's slander.
He summoned Zhào Kuàngzàn's personal troops to the capital,
Zhào Sīwǎn and others were very afraid,
Zhào Sīwǎn,
was a personal officer of Zhào Kuàngzàn,
see previous chapter.
On the road, Sīwǎn said to his associate Cháng Yànqīng:
"The Young Commandant has already fallen into their hands,
Zhào Sīwǎn and others were originally subordinates of Zhào Yánshòu,
therefore they called Kuàngzàn 'Young Commandant',
meaning Kuàngzàn entering the court meant he had already fallen into the Hàn people's hands.
We will die together,
what can we do?"
Yànqīng said:
"Adapt to circumstances as they arise,
say no more!"
On Guǐyǒu,
they reached Cháng'ān,

The 'Háozhài Commissioner' had already arranged lodging quarters east of the city.
Háozhài Commissioner,

The troops under Zhào Sīwǎn had previously followed Zhào Kuàngzàn to garrison Cháng'ān,

Yǒuguī and others agreed.
At that time, Sīwǎn and others all had no armor or weapons,
after entering the west gate,

Sīwǎn suddenly seized his sword and killed him.
His followers therefore raised a great clamor,
seized white clubs,
killed over ten gatekeepers,

Sīwǎn entered the government offices,
opened the armory and distributed armor and weapons to them,
Yǒuguī and others all fled.
Sīwǎn then occupied the city,
gathered the young men of the city,
