Wáng Jǐngchóng hinted to the officials and people of Fèngxiáng to petition for Jǐngchóng to administer the military prefecture,
the court was troubled by this,
on Jiǎxū,

nàn,

Intending to use him to control Wáng Jǐngchóng.
Appointed Jǐngchóng as acting Bīnzhōu Military Commissioner,

The entertainer Jìng Biāntíng of Guó Prefecture killed the militia commissioner Tián Lìngfāng,
drove away and plundered the prefectural people,

Jìng
is a surname.
The names and surnames of entertainers often share a single meaning,

The Comprehensive Account of Customs states: The surname Jìng

Guó Prefecture lies over a hundred li northwest to Tóngguān.
His followers all scattered.

when the Khitan ruler returned north,

the Khitan ruler Déguāng returned north,

This refers to Wùyù returning north to Dìng Prefecture.
He transferred the former military commissioner Sūn Fāngjiǎn to be the military commissioner of Dàtóng.

The Sūn Fāngjiǎn brothers defended Lángshān,

"Shuài"

same below.
The Khitan attacked them,

Yélǜ Zhōng heard that Yèdū had already been pacified,
last November,

An edict appointed Liú Zàimíng, the acting military governor of Chéngdé, as commander of cavalry and infantry of the Yōuzhōu circuit,
ordering him to lead troops to manage Dìng Prefecture.
Before he set out,
Zhōng and Mádá and others burned and plundered Dìng Prefecture,

From Dìng Prefecture east to Zhèn Prefecture,

The Khitan heard that Zhèn Prefecture was about to send out troops,

He returned to occupy Dìng Prefecture,

Whenever the Khitan invaded,
the brothers rushed to respond,
"rushing to respond" means
hurrying to deal with an emergency.
Thus, the prefectures and counties that had fallen to the Khitan by the end of the Jìn

On the bǐngzǐ day,
Liú Zàimíng was appointed military commissioner of Chéngdé.
When Mádá reached his own state,

Mádá was not convinced,

This refers to summoning Féng Dào and others.

6 Sū Féngjí and others, as chancellors,
frequently promoted and appointed many officials;
Yáng Bīn considered this a waste of state resources,
and often suppressed their memorials,
which displeased Féngjí and others.
The Vice Director of the Secretariat and concurrently Minister of Revenue, and participant in determining governmental matters Lǐ Tāo submitted a memorial stating:
"Now the area west of the pass is in turmoil,
and external defense is urgent.
The two Bureau of Military Affairs commissioners are both meritorious officials who assisted the founding,
their offices are noble but their families are not wealthy,
they should be given important frontier commands.
Lǐ Tāo's memorial
followed Sū Féngjí's intention.
The two Bureau of Military Affairs commissioners
refer to Yáng Bīn and Guō Wēi.
It would be easy to make decisions,
Féngjí and Yǔguī have been in office since the previous emperor's time,
and both can be entrusted."
When Yáng Bīn and Guō Wēi heard this,
they went to see the Empress Dowager weeping and complaining,
stating:
"We followed the previous emperor through hardships,
and now the Son of Heaven listens to others' words,
wanting to cast us out to the frontier.
Moreover, there is trouble west of the pass,
meaning Qí and Yōng have raised troops in rebellion.
He does not consider the altars of state.
If we are truly unfit for our posts,
we beg to remain until after the imperial tomb is completed."
The Empress Dowager was angry,
and reprimanded the Emperor,
saying:
"How can you listen to others' words and expel the state's meritorious old ministers!"
The Emperor said:
"This was said by the chancellor."
He then questioned and blamed the chancellor.
Tāo said:
"I alone wrote this memorial,
others were not involved."
On the dīngchǒu day,
Tāo was dismissed from governmental affairs,
and ordered to return to his private residence.
This laid the groundwork for the conflict between generals and ministers.
7 On this day,
the four garrisons of Bīn, Jīng, Tóng, and Huà
Bīn commander Wáng Shǒu'ēn,
Jīng commander Shǐ Kuāngwēi,
Tóng commander Zhāng Yànwēi,
Huà commander Hù Cóngkē.
Huà,
read as "huà."
Zhào Sīwǎn occupied Yǒngxīng,
Wáng Jǐngchóng occupied Fèngxiáng.
Earlier,
when Lǐ Shǒuzhēn heard of Dù Chóngwēi's death, he became fearful,
Dù Chóngwēi's death is recorded in the previous volume, first month of this year.
Considering himself a senior general of the Jìn dynasty,
with military achievements,
Lǐ Shǒuzhēn defeated the Khitan at Mǎjiākǒu and captured Qīng Prefecture,
and also defeated the Khitan at Yángchéng,
his merit was not small.
He had won the hearts of the soldiers.
The Hàn house was newly established,
the Son of Heaven was young and newly enthroned,
those in power were all junior officials,

He then recruited fugitives,
nurtured death-defying warriors,
repaired city moats,
mended armor and weapons,
working day and night without rest.
He sent men by secret paths carrying wax-sealed messages to ally with the Khitan,
but they were repeatedly captured by border officials.
Zhào Xiūjǐ of Jùnyí,
was skilled in divination and numerology,
Old Book of Tang, Treatise on Geography: Jùnyí is an old county,
established in the Sui,
located thirty li north of the current county;
in the fourth year of the Wǔdé era of the Tang,
the county was moved to the inner city north of the prefecture;
in the first year of the Zhēnguān era,
moved to one li west of the prefecture;
later administered from the prefectural seat.
He was appointed Registrar,
and repeatedly followed transfers to different garrisons,
at the beginning of the Kāiyùn era of the Jìn,
Lǐ Shǒuzhēn was garrison commander of Yìchéng,
later transferred to garrison Tàiníng, Tiānpíng, Guīdé,
and by this time was garrison commander of Hùguó and rebelled.
"The time and fate are not right,
do not act recklessly!"
He repeatedly offered earnest remonstrances,
but Shǒuzhēn would not listen,

The monk Zǒnglún,
used his arts to flatter Shǒuzhēn,

With one shot he hit it,

Shǒuzhēn became even more self-assured.
At that time, Zhào Sīwǎn occupied Cháng'ān,

He sent his valiant general Wáng Jìxūn of Pínglù
to occupy Tóngguān.
Old Book of Tang, Treatise on Geography: Pínglù County of Shǎn Prefecture,

Tóngzhōu is closest to Hézhōng,

Sū Féngjí and Sū Yǔguī.

(the three chief ministers:
Dòu Zhèngù, Sū Féngjí, and Sū Yǔguī)

Whenever the three chief ministers proposed candidates for appointment,

Resenting the two Sūs for sidelining him,

To rectify this malpractice,
appointments became difficult,

24. Zhāng Yè, the minister of works and concurrently vice director of the Secretariat and chief minister of Shǔ,
was extravagant by nature,
forcibly buying people's land and houses,
using his power to oppress others.
People feared his power,
and had no choice but to engage in transactions with him,
which constituted forced buying.
He established a prison,
detaining debtors for years,
some even dying from illness.
(Sū Lín said: Yǔ
means illness.
When prisoners fall ill,
it is termed yǔ in legal terms.
Rú Chún said: According to the law, prisoners dying from hunger or cold is called yǔ.
Pronounced yǒng zhǔ fān.)
He enjoyed sword fighting,
and once visited a monk named Guīxìn to seek skilled swordsmen.
Sūn Hànsháo, the deputy commander of the Right Kuāngshèng army, had a grudge against Yè,

Lǐ Hào, the academician recipient of edicts, and Ān Sīqiān, the commander of the Fèngshèng Kònghè cavalry and infantry, further slandered them.
On Jiǎzǐ,
when Yè attended court,
the ruler of Shǔ ordered strong men to kill him in the main hall,
issued an edict exposing his crimes,

Wáng Chùhuí, the privy councilor, military commissioner of Bǎoníng, and concurrently palace attendant,

not stationed in Làng Prefecture.)
Tributes from all directions
were first delivered to Chùhuí,
and only then to the imperial treasury.
(The term "all directions" here
refers only to the borders of Shǔ.)
His son Déjūn
was also arrogant and tyrannical.
After Zhāng Yè's death,
the ruler of Shǔ could not bear to kill Chùhuí,

The ruler of Shǔ intended to appoint Pǔfēng Treasury Commissioner Gāo Yánzhāo and Tea and Wine Treasury Commissioner Wáng Zhāoyuǎn as Commissioners of the Bureau of Military Affairs.
The positions of Pǔfēng and Tea and Wine Treasury Commissioners
were both established by Shǔ.
He then appointed them as Commissioners of General Memorials,
in charge of the Bureau of Military Affairs.
The position of Commissioner of General Memorials
was also established by Shǔ.
Wáng Zhāoyuǎn was a native of Chéngdū.
As a child, he entered the government office as a novice monk accompanying his master.
The founding emperor of Shǔ admired his intelligence and cleverness,
and ordered him to serve by the ruler's side.
By this time,
he was entrusted with confidential affairs,
and the gold and silk in the government treasury
were allowed to be taken and given at his discretion,

On the 25th day, Wùchén,
Guō Cóngyì was appointed as Military Commissioner of Yǒngxīng,

At that time, Guō Cóngyì was campaigning against Cháng'ān,

Bái Wénkē was campaigning against Hézhōng,

On the 26th, the ruler of Shǔ appointed Hanlin Academician Recipient of Edicts and Vice Director of the Left of the Department of State Affairs Lǐ Hào as Vice Director of the Chancellery and concurrently Minister of Revenue,
and Hanlin Academician and Vice Minister of War Xú Guāngpǔ as Vice Director of the Secretariat and concurrently Minister of Rites,
both also as Tongpingzhangshi (Participating in Determining Governmental Matters).
On the 27th, Ān Sīqiān of Shǔ plotted to completely remove the old generals,
and also slandered the Imperial Guard Commander and concurrently Zhongshuling (Director of the Secretariat) Zhào Tíngyǐn for plotting rebellion,
intending to take his position.
At night,
he dispatched troops to surround Zhào's residence.
It happened that the Military Commissioner of Shānnánxīdào Lǐ Tíngguī was coming to court,
and he strongly argued that Zhào Tíngyǐn was innocent,
so Zhào was spared.
Zhào Tíngyǐn then claimed illness,
and firmly requested to be relieved of his military duties.
On the Jiǎxū day,
the ruler of Shǔ granted his request.
The history states that the ruler of Shǔ used new officials to alienate the old ones.
On the 28th, the Military Commissioner of Fèngxiáng Zhào Huī arrived in Cháng'ān.
On the Yǐhài day,
he submitted a memorial stating that Wáng Jǐngchóng's signs of rebellion were increasingly evident,
and requested to advance troops to attack him.
Earlier,
when the founding emperor was stationed in Hédōng,
his younger brother Chóng was the Commander of the Horse and Foot Troops,
and contended for power with the Director of the Bureau of Barbarian and Han Affairs Guō Wēi,
creating a rift between them.
When Guō Wēi came to power,
Chóng became worried.
The Administrative Assistant of the Military Commissioner Zhèng Gǒng
advised Chóng to make plans for self-preservation,
and Chóng followed his advice.
Zhèng Gǒng
was from Qīngzhōu.
In the eighth month,
on the Gēngchén day,
Chóng submitted a memorial requesting to recruit four battalions of troops.
From then on, he selected and recruited brave warriors,
gathered fugitives,
repaired armor and weapons,
filled the government treasury,
and suspended the delivery of taxes and tributes to the court,
all under the pretext of preparing against the Qìdān.
He often did not comply with
the court's edicts and orders.
At this time,
Liú Chóng was acting arrogantly and defiantly.
However, after Guō Wēi established himself,
and the realm became Zhōu,
if Hédōng had not been prepared beforehand,
it likely could not have been held.
Since the three military towns of Hézhōng, Yǒngxīng, and Fèngxiáng defied orders,
the court successively dispatched various generals to campaign against them.
The Military Commissioner of Zhāoyì Cháng Sī was stationed at Tóngguān,
Bái Wénkē at Tóngzhōu,
and Zhào Huī at Xiányáng.
Cháng Sī and Bái Wénkē did not dare to press Hézhōng,
and Zhào Huī did not dare to press Fèngxiáng.
Moreover, the two men hated each other like fire and water,
and from spring to autumn,
they both relied on each other but were unwilling to attack and fight.
The emperor was troubled by this,
and wanted to send a high-ranking minister to oversee and supervise.
On the Rénwǔ day,
he appointed Guō Wēi as the Western Front Commissioner for Pacification and Appeasement.
Textual analysis notes: The History of the Five Dynasties, Chronicle of Tàizǔ of Zhōu states:
"On the 13th day of the seventh month,
he was appointed as Tongpingzhangshi,
and was immediately sent on the western campaign,
under the name of appeasement and pacification.
He departed on the sixth day of the eighth month,
leaving the capital."
According to the Veritable Records of Emperor Yǐn of Hàn and Tàizǔ of Zhōu,
"In the seventh month,
he was appointed as Tongpingzhangshi,"
but the appointment edict contained no mention of a western campaign.
It was not until the Rénwǔ day of the eighth month
that he received orders to campaign.
This is likely an error in the History of the Five Dynasties.
Before Guō Wēi departed,
he sought advice from Grand Preceptor Féng Dào.
Féng Dào said:
"Lǐ Shǒuzhēn considers himself a veteran general,
and is supported by the soldiers.
I hope you, sir, will not be sparing with government property,
but bestow it upon the soldiers.
Then you will take away what he relies on."
Guō Wēi followed this advice.
Guō Wēi, a hero among the soldiers,
sought advice from the old and pedantic Féng Dào.
Observing the answer he gave and why Guō Wēi followed it,
it shows that in terms of talent and insight,
there may be those who do not conform to the Way,
but in assessing situations and responding to circumstances,
one should not make rash judgments.
This sets the stage for Guō Wēi's eventual gaining of the realm.
An edict ordered Bái Wénkē to advance toward Hézhōng,
and Zhào Huī to advance toward Fèngxiáng.
On the 31st, Jiǎshēn day,
the ruler of Shǔ appointed Zhào Tíngyǐn as Grand Mentor,
bestowed upon him the title of Prince of Sòng,

Examination of discrepancies says: The Veritable Records,

meaning twenty to thirty thousand men,
which was no small campaign,

Killing three thousand men,

before he could cross the border.
The Shǔ sovereign said:
"Judging from Sīqiān's intention,
how could he possibly advance and attack for Us!"
Nevertheless, he also dispatched tens of thousands of hú of rice from Xīngzhōu and Xīngyuán to supply him.
On Wùzǐ,
Sīqiān advanced and stationed at Sànguān.
He sent the Cavalry and Infantry Officer Gāo Yànchóu and the Prefect of Méizhōu, Shēn Guì, to attack the Hàn's Jiànkuò Āndū Fortress,
and defeated it.

Sīqiān defeated Hàn troops at Yùnǚ Tán.

Hán Bǎozhēn exited Xīnguān,
Xīnguān is west of Qiānyuán County, Lǒngzhōu.
In the sixth year of Dàzhōng of the Táng dynasty,
the Lǒngzhōu Defense Commissioner Xuē Kuí relocated and built it,

The people of Qiān and Lǒng called Dàzhèn the old pass,

*Jiǔyù Zhì*: Qiānyuán County, Lǒngzhōu, has a Xīnguān town.
On Rénchén,
he stationed his army at Shénqián in Lǒngzhōu.
The Hàn troops did not come out,

"Móbì",

"Mōbì".
Zhào Huī urgently appealed to Guō Wēi for help,

At that time, Lǐ Shǒuzhēn had sent his Deputy Commissioner Zhōu Guāngxùn, Vice General Wáng Jìxūn, and Niè Zhīyù to defend the west of the city.
Wēi cautioned Bái Wénkē and Liú Cí, saying:
"If the rebels cannot break through the encirclement,

If by any chance they manage to break out,

The moment of success or failure
lies precisely in this.
The enemy's most valiant and elite troops
are all in the west of the city.
Once I leave, they are sure to come and attempt a breakout.
You must be carefully prepared for this!"
When Wēi reached Huázhōu,
he heard that the Shǔ troops had exhausted their provisions and withdrawn.
*Kǎoyì* says: *Shíguó Jìnián* records:
"In the first month, on Jiǎyǐn, in the twelfth year of the Guǎngzhèng era of Shǔ,

retreated from Móbì and stationed at Fèngzhōu,
submitting a memorial awaiting punishment."
It seems that by the end of last winter, the army had already retreated,
and the memorial reached Chéngdū only in the first month of the following year.
Now we follow the *Zhōu Tàizǔ Shílù*.
Hán Bǎozhēn, hearing that Ān Sīqiān had left,
also retreated and defended Gōngchuān Fortress.
*Jiǔyù Zhì*: There is a Gōngmén Fortress 165 lǐ east of Qínzhōu.

The Vice Director of the Central Secretariat and Minister of Rites of Shu, concurrently Tongpingzhangshi Xú Guāngpǔ, was accused of using flirtatious language to seduce the Former Shu Princess of Ānkāng.
On Dīngyǒu,
he was dismissed from his additional post and retained only his original official position.
Second year of Qiányòu (Jǐyǒu, 949)
1. Spring,
first month,
Yǐsì, the first day.
A general amnesty was proclaimed.
2. Guō Wēi was about to reach Hézhōng,
having returned from Huázhōu.
On the night of Wùshēn,
Lǐ Shǒuzhēn dispatched Wáng Jìxūn and others to lead over a thousand elite troops south along the river,
to raid the Hàn army's stockade.
They cut steps into the riverbank and climbed up,
thus entering it.
This was the Hàn army's stockade west of the river.
Wáng Jìxūn knew that the Hàn troops occupied the west bank of the river, overlooking the east bank,
and their defenses were certainly strong.
Therefore, he went south along the river,
cut steps into the bank and ascended to attack them.
The army was in disarray and did not know what to do.
Liú Cí's expression remained calm.
He issued an order:
"These petty bandits are not enough to cause alarm."
He led the troops to attack them.
The Commissioner of Guest Reception Yán Jìnqīng said:
The Liáng had Commissioners and Vice Commissioners of Guest Reception;
the Sòng followed this system.
They were in charge of matters concerning tribute from all regions and foreign states, visits and tributes from regional chiefs and nobles, bestowal of wine and food,
and the granting of gifts and returning of edicts to chief ministers, close officials, imperial guard commanders and officers, military ranks, and tribute envoys from various prefectures.
"The enemy's armor is all made of yellow paper,

making it easy to identify;
but what can be done when our troops lack the will to fight!"
Deputy General Lǐ Tāo said:

Seizing a lance, he advanced first,
and the others followed him.
The Hézhōng troops retreated and fled,

Jìxūn was severely wounded,

On Jǐyǒu,
Guō Wēi arrived.

Guō Wēi rewarded him generously,

"My worry was precisely this.

wēi,

thus allowing the Hézhōng troops to secretly enter the camp,

drank a little wine in the morning.

Shǎo,

"You serve under my command,

3. On Jiǎyǐn,
Shǔ's Ān Sīqiān retreated and stationed at Fèngzhōu.
He submitted a memorial awaiting punishment,

Those who hesitate or are cowardly in military operations must be executed;
pardoning and not inquiring is a failure of justice.

The Táng established the Dudu of Jìngbiānzhōu within the boundaries of Yínzhōu,

Nàn,

Yíyīn, due to the many troubles in the Central Plains,
developed an attitude of contempt and arrogance.
Whenever a military governor rebelled,
he often secretly aided them,
demanding heavy bribes.
The court knew of these matters,
but also used favors to keep him under control.
The history states that the Tuòbá clan occupied Yín and Xià,

5. Many bandits north of the Huái River requested allegiance to the Táng.
The Táng ruler dispatched the Commander of the Divine Guard, Huángfǔ Huī, and others to lead ten thousand troops out of Hǎi and Sì to recruit and accept them.
Huángfǔ Huī
was the one who, together with Zhào Zàilǐ, caused the rebellion that led to the disaster for Later Táng Zhuāngzōng;

Hǎi and Sì

Jiǔyù Zhì: It is 160 lǐ south of the prefecture.
Six hundred were captured or beheaded,

The Khitan ruler agreed,

Ōu Shǐ says: Traveling 1,200 lǐ southeast from Liáoyáng Prefecture to reach Jiànzhōu.

North of the Tǔ River is the Khitan's Central Capital, Dàdìng Prefecture.
Dàdìng Prefecture is 1,150 lǐ south to Yānjīng,

The Jīn people's territorial map: Jiànzhōu is 1,245 lǐ south to Yānjīng.

Ān Tài died on the road.
He left instructions:

They received over 50 qǐng of land.

Jǐwèi.

Zhì,

Rénwǔ.
Venus was visible during the day;

10. In Hézhōng City, food was nearly exhausted,

Zhōu Guāngxùn, Wáng Jìxūn, and Niè Zhīyù led their followers, over a thousand men, to surrender.
Zhōu Guāngxùn and Wáng Jìxūn
were Lǐ Shǒuzhēn’s valiant generals.
The character “shuài”
is read as “lead.”
Guō Wēi, taking advantage of their dispersal,
on Gēngshēn,
commanded the various armies to attack from a hundred directions.
This was the old strategy Sima Wénwáng used to capture Zhūgě Dàn.
11. Zhào Sīwǎn enjoyed eating human livers;
he would personally slice them open and cut them into thin slices,
and even after the slicing was finished,
the person would still not be dead.
He also liked to swallow human gallbladders with wine,
saying to people:
“If I swallow a thousand of these,
then my gallbladder will be invincible.”
When food in Cháng'ān City was exhausted,
he took women and children as military provisions,
counting them daily and distributing them accordingly.
Whenever he rewarded the army,
he would slaughter several hundred people,
treating them like sheep and pigs.
Sīwǎn’s schemes were exhausted,
and he did not know what to do.
Guō Cóngyì sent someone to lure him.
Earlier,
when Sīwǎn was young,
he sought to become the servant of the retired Left Xiaowei Superior General Lǐ Sù,
but Sù did not accept him,
saying:
“This man’s eyes are wild and his speech is extravagant;
someday he will surely become a rebel.”
Sù’s wife, née Zhāng,
was the daughter of Zhāng Quányì.
Zhāng Quányì governed Luò,
and established merit and fame between the Liáng and Táng dynasties.
“If you refuse him now,
he will later bring trouble.”
So she generously gave him gold and silk.
When Sīwǎn occupied Cháng'ān,
Sù was living in retirement in the city.
Sīwǎn visited him several times,
bowing and prostrating himself according to the old etiquette.
In the twelfth year of Tiānfú,
Zhào Zàilǐ went from Cháng'ān to pay court to the Qìdān,
and his subordinate generals who remained in Cháng'ān started a rebellion.
Lǐ Sù suppressed and executed them,
which shows his prestige must have been considerable.
Zhào Sīwǎn also remembered the past kindness he had received,
so even though he had usurped power,
when he saw Sù, he still behaved with the etiquette of a servant serving his master.
The character “shuò”
is pronounced as “shuài.”
“This fellow keeps coming,
and will defile me.”
He wanted to commit suicide.
His wife said:
“Why not persuade him to return to the state!”
History records that Lǐ Sù’s wife was wise.
Sù then, together with his administrative assistant Chéng Ràngnéng, advised Sīwǎn, saying:
“You originally had no grievance with the state,
but only feared punishment.
Now the state is using troops on three fronts,
all without success.”
The three fronts using troops
refer to Guō Wēi attacking Hézhōng,
Zhào Huī attacking Fèngxiáng,
and Guō Cóngyì attacking Sīwǎn.
“If you now turn back and submit,
the court will surely be pleased,
and you can naturally retain wealth and honor.
How can this compare to sitting and waiting for death!”
Sīwǎn followed this advice,
and sent an envoy to the capital requesting surrender.
On Yǐchǒu,
Sīwǎn was appointed as Liúhòu of Huázhōu,
that is, Liúhòu of the Zhènguó Army.
He was ordered to take office directly.
Not allowing him to enter the court was to pacify his wavering heart.

a partisan of Hú Jìnsī,

Guō Wēi attacked Hézhōng,

Lǐ Shǒuzhēn gathered his remaining troops,

The generals requested an urgent attack,

To catch fish by draining the pond,

On Rénxū,
Lǐ Shǒuzhēn, together with his wife and son Chóngxūn and others, burned themselves to death.

sent them to Dàliáng,

Jìng
is the surname;
is his given name.
is pronounced tóng dū fān,

Because Zhào Xiūjǐ had repeatedly admonished Lǐ Shǒuzhēn.
In Shèngtáng, there were astronomical doctors and astronomical students,

Wēi examined Shǒuzhēn’s documents,

to pacify those with wavering hearts.”

Guō Wēi’s western campaign,

How could this be matched by any stubborn military man of the time!
After the three rebellions were pacified,

He became intimate with those around him.
Feilongshǐ Xiàqiū Hòu Kuāngzàn

and the emperor enjoyed exchanging riddles and vulgar language with them.
Riddles,

Enjoy,

Riddle,

The emperor did not take it seriously.
On Guǐhài,

He did not listen.

17 On Wùchén,

18 The Southern Táng ruler reappointed Wèi Cén;

He participated in state affairs;

Fàn Chōngmǐn, a vice director in the Ministry of Revenue,

When the Southern Táng ruler heard that Hézhōng had fallen,

The Wénlǐ Academy
was established by the Southern Táng.
Vice directors in the Ministry of Personnel had no specific bureau duties,

19 Wúyuè King Qián Hóngchù appointed his chancellor Qián Hóngyì as prefect of Míngzhōu.
This was because of the Tǒu Tāo affair that Hóngyì was sent out.
20 Wáng Shǒu'ēn, the defender of the Western Capital and tóng píngzhāng shì,
was greedy and despicable by nature,

Nightsoil,

In August,

Shěn Kuò said: After Emperor Zhuāngzōng of Later Táng restored the position of Privy Councilor,

Shǒu'ēn was still sitting in the guest quarters,
guest quarters,

"The new defender has already assumed duties at the headquarters."

Ōuyáng Xiū commented: Since ancient times, states that fell into chaos and ruin
inevitably first had their legal systems corrupted
before chaos followed,
which is the natural tendency,
as seen in the Five Dynasties period.
Wénkē and Shǒu'ēn were both great ministers of Hàn,
yet Zhōu Tàizǔ, as a single Privy Councilor, used a headnote to replace them,
as if changing garrison troops.
At that time, Tàizǔ had no intention of disloyalty to the sovereign,
yet he acted this way
because it had become customary,
so Wénkē dared not disobey,
and Shǒu'ēn dared not resist.
Since Tàizǔ handled it without suspicion,
and the Hàn court officials also ignored it,
was this not because the legal order was utterly corrupted and chaotic to this extent!
I note that at the beginning of Emperor Mǐn of Táng,
Zhū Hóngzhāo and Féng Bīn used Privy Council decrees to replace various military governors,
leading to the rebellion of the Prince of Lù,
and though the outcomes differed,
the heavy authority of the Privy Council had its origins.
One must not neglect the subtle and always prevent its gradual development,
should this not be a warning!

The Fángyùshǐ of various prefectures in the Five Dynasties period were not even comparable to the Hàn Dynasty's two-thousand-dàn commandery governors.

Yáng Bīn requested to be relieved of his duties as Privy Councilor,

Wèi,
pronounced yú wèi.
"These are matters of state,
why take them to heart!"
Hóngzhào again said sternly:
"To stabilize the state,
we rely on long spears and great swords,
what use are writing brushes!"
Wáng Zhāng said:
"Without writing brushes,
from where would revenue and taxes come?"
"Máo zhuī" refers to writing brushes;
brushes made of bundled hair,
shaped like an awl.
Wáng Zhāng was the Commissioner of the Three Departments,
actually in charge of revenue and taxes,
hence he spoke thus.
On the 22nd day, Guǐwèi,
the Yǒng'ān Army was abolished.
Fǔzhōu was again placed under Hédōng.
On the first day of the fifth month, Jǐhài,
the Fǔzhōu Tribal and Chinese Cavalry and Infantry Commander Shé Déyǐ was appointed as the local Regimental Training Commissioner.
Previously, the Yǒng'ān Army had been established in Fǔzhōu,
to honor Shé Cóngruǎn.
Now that Cóngruǎn had been transferred,
his son Déyǐ defended Fǔzhōu,
his seniority not yet sufficient,
and Fǔzhōu being a single border city,
he was thus demoted to Regimental Training Commissioner.
Later it was again made a military command,
to honor the Shé family.
He was the son of Cóngruǎn.
On the 11th day, Rénchén,
Zuǒ Jiānménwèi General Guō Róng was appointed as Guìzhōu Prefect and Tiānxióng Yá-Nèi Capital Commandant.
Guìzhōu at that time belonged to the Southern Hàn.
Sòng Bái said: Guìzhōu,
was originally the land of the Western Ōu and Luòyuè peoples,
although the Qín established the Guìlín Commandery,
the names Ōu and Luòyuè remained,
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn changed Guìlín to the Yùlín Commandery,
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng changed the Yùlín Commandery to Guìzhōu,
later the Yùlín and Níngpǔ areas of Guìzhōu were separated to establish Dìngzhōu,
soon changed to Nándìngzhōu,
Suí changed Nándìngzhōu to Yǐnzhōu,
Táng changed it to Guìzhōu.
The Hàn appointed Guō Róng as a nominal Prefect,
but his actual duty was as a Tiānxióng Yá general.
Textual analysis note: The Shízōng Shílù says:
"He was the eldest son of Emperor Tàizǔ,

The Shǐzōng Annals of the Old History of the Five Dynasties says:

Note: Now the whole world knows that Shǐzōng was the son of the Chái family,
called Chái Shǐzōng;
yet the Shǐzōng Shílù says he was the eldest son of Emperor Tàizǔ,
the falsification is extreme.
His father Shǒulǐ,

Wēi adopted him as a son when he had no sons.
Guō Róng first appears here.
In the fifth month,
on the 8th day, Jǐhài,
the Fǔzhōu Tribal and Chinese Cavalry and Infantry Commander Shé Déyǐ was appointed as the local Regimental Training Commissioner.
On the 23rd day, Gēngzǐ,
Guō Wēi took his leave and departure.
He addressed the Emperor, saying:
"The Empress Dowager has long accompanied the late Emperor
and has experienced many affairs of the realm.
Your Majesty is in the spring and autumn of your life,
and in matters of governance, it is appropriate to receive her instruction and act accordingly.
Draw near to the loyal and upright,
and keep far away from the slanderous and wicked.
Between good and evil,
it is fitting to be clear and discerning.
Sū Féngjí, Yáng Bīn, and Shǐ Hóngzhào are all former ministers of the late Emperor,
who have exhausted their loyalty and sacrificed themselves for the state.
I hope Your Majesty will trust them wholeheartedly and employ them,
and there will certainly be no failures or losses.
Guō Wēi spoke of this
because he already knew that the Emperor trusted those close to him and distanced himself from the meritorious veterans.
Your servant wishes to exhaust his foolish and mediocre abilities,
hoping not to fail the driving whip."
The Emperor composed his expression and thanked him.
Guō Wēi arrived at Yèdū.
Because Héběi was impoverished and depleted,
he warned the border generals to strictly guard the frontiers,
maintain strict defenses,
and not go out to invade or plunder.
If the Khitan invaded,
they were to fortify their positions and clear the fields to await them.
This is what military strategy calls "first make yourself invincible, then wait for the enemy to become vulnerable."
On the 24th day, Xīnchǒu,
an edict was issued:
"Defense Commissioners and Militia Training Commissioners,
unless it is a military matter requiring immediate action,
may not submit memorials directly.
They must first report to the Observation Commissioner for consideration before it is presented."
This meant that if a military matter required immediate response from the court,
and there was no time to inform the Surveillance Commissioner,
they were permitted to report directly to the court.
As for ordinary public affairs,
they must first be reported to their superior for consideration before being presented.
On the 25th day, Bǐngwǔ,
the Emperor's younger brother, Chéngxūn, Military Commissioner of Shānnánxī Circuit, was appointed Prefect of Kāifēng,
and additionally granted the concurrent title of Secretariat Director.
In reality, he had not yet left the palace.
He was still young,
and moreover had a weak constitution and illness.
Shānnánxī Circuit was at that time within Shǔ territory.
On the 26th, Liú Zhū, Military Commissioner of Pínglú,
was greedy, cruel, and arbitrary;
the court wished to summon him,
but feared he would refuse the order.
Because troops were being used against Táng in Yí and Mì,
they sent Guō Qióng, Prefect of Yí Province, to lead troops and station them in Qīngzhōu.
The Ouyáng History states: Guō Huái, after attacking Southern Táng and returning,
stationed troops in Qīngzhōu.
Liú Zhū prepared a banquet and summoned Guō Qióng.
He hid soldiers behind the curtains,
intending to harm him.
Guō Qióng knew of his plot,
dismissed all his attendants,
and calmly attended the meeting,
showing not the slightest fear.
Liú Zhū did not dare to act.
Guō Qióng then explained to him the consequences of fortune and misfortune.
Liú Zhū was moved and submitted.
When the imperial edict arrived, he departed immediately.
On the Gēngxū day,
Liú Zhū entered the court.
On the Xīnhài day,
Guō Qióng was appointed Militia Training Commissioner of Yǐngzhōu.
On the 27th day, Guǐchǒu,
Wáng Zhāng hosted a banquet for the various court dignitaries.
When the wine was in full swing,
they played the hand gesture drinking game.
Drinking together and playing drinking games to enhance enjoyment
was a custom of the late Táng period.
The Lèi Shuō states:
"Press the tiger's chest,"
refers to the palm.
"Bend the pine root,"
refers to the finger joints.
"Place the squatting owl between the tiger's chest,"
the squatting owl
is the thumb.
"Place the hook halberd beside the jade pillar,"
the hook halberd
is the index finger;
the jade pillar,
is the middle finger.
"The hidden dragon is three-tenths wider than the jade pillar,"
the hidden dragon,
is the ring finger.
"The surprise troops are one inch wider than the hidden dragon,"
the surprise troops,
is the little finger.
"Kill its three rivers,"
means to droop the wrist.
"Give life to its five peaks,"
the five peaks,
collectively refer to the five fingers.
This is called the beckoning game.
It is probably also a type of hand gesture game!
It is said that he was not accustomed to such activities.
They repeatedly taught him.
Sū Féngjí teased him, saying:
"There is a person surnamed Yán beside you,
why worry about penalty drinks!"
The matter of pot shooting,
where the loser is penalized with drinks,
has existed since ancient times,
but playing drinking games is a practice of later ages.
He was originally a singing girl from a tavern,
and thinking that Sū Féngjí was mocking him,
he became greatly enraged,
and reviled Sū Féngjí with foul language.
Sū Féngjí did not respond.
Shǐ Hóngzhào wanted to beat him,
but Sū Féngjí rose and left.
Shǐ Hóngzhào sought a sword to pursue him,
but Yáng Bīn tearfully stopped him, saying:
"Lord Sū is the Chancellor.
If you, sir, kill him,
what place would that leave for the Son of Heaven?
I beg you to consider this carefully!"
Shú
is the same as shú (thoroughly).
Yáng Bīn rode side by side with him,
escorted him to his residence, and then returned.
From then on, the generals and ministers were like fire and water.
The Emperor sent Wáng Jùn, the Commissioner of the Palace Reception, to host a banquet to reconcile them,
but he could not succeed.
Sū Féngjí wished to request an appointment outside the capital to avoid him,
but after a while he stopped,
saying:
"If I leave the court,
it would only take one disposition from Lord Shǐ,
and I would be ground to powder!"
Wáng Zhāng was also dispirited and unhappy,
and wished to seek an official post outside the capital,
but Yáng and Shǐ firmly stopped him.
In the intercalary month,
there were several strange occurrences in the palace.
On the Guǐsì day,
a great wind arose,
tearing off roofs and uprooting trees.
It blew the gate of the Zhèng Gate off its hinges,
carrying it more than ten paces before it fell,
killing six or seven people by the impact,
and the water rose over a foot above the ground.
The Emperor summoned Zhào Yányì, the Director of the Astrological Service,
and asked him about methods of exorcism and prayer.
He replied:
"Your servant's profession lies in astronomy and calendrical matters;
exorcism and prayer are not what I have studied.
However, if the ruler wishes to dispel calamities and anomalies,
there is nothing better than cultivating virtue."
After Zhào Yányì returned,
the Emperor sent a palace envoy to ask:
"How does one cultivate virtue?"
Zhào Yányì replied:
"I request that you read the Zhēnguàn Zhèngyào and emulate it."
In the sixth month,
the Yellow River breached at Zhèngzhōu.
The Ouyáng History states: In the sixth month,
on the Guǐmǎo day,
the Yellow River breached at Yuánwǔ.
According to records, Yuánwǔ County belonged to Zhèngzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Yuánwǔ County is sixty lǐ north of Zhèngzhōu.
On the 30th, Mǎ Xī'è, after being defeated and returning—
the defeat at Púshè Zhōu,
the event is recorded in the previous volume, last year in the eighth month—
wished to join forces with him to attack Húnán.
The Man tribes had long heard of the wealth stored in Chángshā's treasuries,
and were greatly pleased,
vying to send troops to join him.
They then attacked Yìyáng.
Yìyáng County
belonged to Tánzhōu.
The old Hàn county town was located eighty lǐ east of the Táng county town.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Yìyáng is 182 lǐ northwest of Tánzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Because the place was located on the north bank of the Yì River,
it was so named.
Its city walls were built by Lǔ Sù.
They fought at Yānxī,
and Fán was defeated and died.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
Táng returned Mǎ Xiānjìn and others to Wúyuè in exchange for Chá Wénhuī.
Mǎ Xiānjìn and others being captured is recorded in the previous volume, in the second month of this year.
Chá Wénhuī was also captured by Wúyuè in this month.
Since the Emperor's accession to the throne,
the Privy Councilor, Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, and Co-Manager of Affairs with the Secretariat-Chancellery Yáng Bīn had overseen the administration of state affairs;
the Privy Councilor and concurrently Palace Attendant Guō Wēi had been in charge of military campaigns;
the Military Commissioner of Guide, Commander of the Palace Guard, and concurrently Director of the Secretariat Shǐ Hóngzhào had been responsible for the palace guard;
the Three Fiscal Commissioners and Co-Manager of Affairs with the Secretariat-Chancellery Wáng Zhāng had managed finances and taxation.
Yáng Bīn was quite impartial and loyal;
after retiring from court,
his gate saw no private visits;
although he did not refuse gifts from all quarters,
any surplus was always presented to the state.
Shǐ Hóngzhào oversaw the capital,
and lost items were not picked up on the roads.
At this time, following the devastation wrought by the Khitan,
when the Khitan entered Biàn,
the Central Plains were laid waste.
After the Khitan withdrew north,
the Hàn succeeded them.
Wáng Zhāng gathered leftover profits,
was frugal in expenditures,
and filled the treasury.
During the period when three rebellions formed an alliance,
troops were stationed for years, yet supplies were never lacking;
after the matters were pacified,
aside from rewards and grants,
there was still surplus accumulation,
so the state was somewhat stable.
Wáng Zhāng's taxation was harsh and urgent.
According to the old system,
for each hú of land tax, an additional two shēng were levied,
called
"sparrow and rodent wastage";
Wáng Zhāng first ordered an additional two dǒu to be levied,
called
"provincial wastage";
according to the amnesty decree of the first year of Tiānchéng of Táng Míngzōng in the fourth month:
"For those who should pay summer and autumn taxes,
there was previously provincial wastage,
one shēng per dǒu;
from now on, only the proper tax amount shall be paid,
without measuring provincial wastage."
Thus,
before Tiānchéng, there was already provincial wastage,
with an additional one dǒu per hú,
and Tiānchéng abolished this levy.
Later, when the Hàn arose,
Wáng Zhāng again ordered the payment of provincial wastage,
and moreover doubled the old amount to collect it.
Wáng Zhāng first ordered that for every eighty received,
seventy-seven were disbursed,
called
"provincial mò";
Shěn Kuò said: Nowadays, counting one hundred coins is called
"mò",
borrowing
the character
"mò"
for use,
but it actually just means
"hundred",
like
"shí"
and
"wǔ"
and
"ěr".
Since Huángfǔ Bó of the Táng implemented the method of padding money,
by the time of Emperor Zhāozōng,
it was set that eighty was a mò.
Even the slightest bit,
was punishable by death;
the salt prohibition had long been established;
as for the prohibition on alcohol,
sometimes abolished, sometimes monopolized,
it was inconsistent throughout the generations.
Since the mid-Táng, the prohibition on alcohol monopoly began to be enforced,
and by its end, the making of yeast was also prohibited.
As for the prohibition on alum,
the Old and New Táng Books' Treatises on Food and Money did not mention it,
so it must have started at the beginning of the Five Dynasties.
The Illustrated Classic of Materia Medica says: Alum stone,
is produced in the valleys of Héxī and in Wǔdū and Shímén of Lǒngxī.
Nowadays, white alum comes from Jìnzhōu, Cízhōu, Gǒngzhōu, and Wúwéi Jūn,
green alum comes from Wēnquán County of Xízhōu and Tónglíng County of Chízhōu, where alum is boiled,
and it is produced everywhere.
Initially, it is all stone,
which is mined and crushed,
then boiled and refined to become alum.
There are five types in total,
each with different colors,
called white alum, green alum, yellow alum, black alum, and crimson alum.
From Qí Bó to Táo Yǐnjū's writings, all mention it.
Wáng Zhāng particularly disliked civil officials,
once saying:
"If you give these people an abacus,
they wouldn't know how to use it,
what use are they!"
Their salaries were all given with items unfit for military use,
and the officials had already inflated their valuations,
but Wáng Zhāng increased them further.
Valuation,
means price.
The Emperor's favored attendants gradually gained influence,
and the Empress Dowager's relatives also interfered in court affairs,
which Yáng Bīn and others repeatedly restrained.
The Empress Dowager had the son of an old acquaintance seeking a military post,
and Shǐ Hóngzhào angrily executed him.
The Military Commissioner of Wǔdé Lǐ Yè,
was the Empress Dowager's younger brother,
the Empress Dowager had seven brothers,
and Lǐ Yè was the youngest,
so she especially doted on him.
After the Emperor ascended the throne,
he was particularly favored and trusted.
When the position of Palace Attendant became vacant,
Lǐ Yè desired it,
Wú Qiányù was sent out to Zhèngzhōu,
leaving the position of Palace Attendant of the Northern Bureau vacant.
Yáng Bīn and Shǐ Hóngzhào believed that promotions within the palace service followed an order,
and an imperial relative could not leap ahead,
so it was stopped.
The Palace Reception Commissioner Yán Jìnqīng was next in line to become Palace Attendant,
but it remained unfilled for a long time;
the Privy Council Recipient of Edicts Niè Wénjìn, the Flying Dragon Commissioner Hòu Kuāngzàn, and the Hanlin Tea and Wine Commissioner Guō Yǔnmíng were all favored by the Emperor,
but had not been promoted for a long time,
and together resented those in power.
The Genealogy of Surnames says: The surname Hòu,
has its prominent branches in Dōnghǎi and Kāifēng.
He was from Bīngzhōu.
Liú Zhū was dismissed from Qīngzhōu and returned,
had long attended court audiences,
but was not appointed to an official post,
often shaking his fist at those in power.
In the summer of this year, in the fifth month,
Liú Zhū was summoned back from Qīngzhōu.
Shaking his fist means,
shaking his hand and cursing in resentment.
The emperor had just concluded the three-year mourning period,
and was enjoying music.
He bestowed brocade robes and jade belts upon the musicians.
The musicians went to Shǐ Hóngzhào to express their thanks.
Hóngzhào angrily said:
"The soldiers guarding the frontiers endure bitter battles,
yet they have not received such gifts.
What merit do you all have to receive these?"
He seized the gifts and returned them to the authorities.
The emperor wished to establish his favored consort, Gěng Fūrén, as empress.
Yáng Bīn considered it too hasty.
When the lady died,
the emperor wished to bury her with the rites of an empress.
Bīn again considered it improper.
As the emperor grew older and stronger,
he grew weary of being controlled by his ministers.
Bīn and Hóngzhào were once discussing matters before the emperor.
The emperor said:
"Consider this carefully,
do not let people have cause for criticism!"
Bīn said:
"Your Majesty should just remain silent."
"Remain silent"
means to keep one's mouth shut and not speak,
so that no sound is uttered.
The emperor's accumulated resentment could not be appeased.
His attendants seized the opportunity to slander them to the emperor,
saying:
"Bīn and the others are arbitrary and domineering,
and will eventually rebel."
The emperor believed them.
He once heard at night the sound of forging from the workshops.
Workshops
are places where weapons and armor are made,
overseen by the Workshop Commissioner.
Forging
(pronounced duàn).
It means forging iron to make weapons and armor.
He stayed awake until dawn.
The Minister of Works and Tongpingzhangshi Sū Féngjí, having already developed a rift with Hóngzhào,
knew that Lǐ Yè and others resented Hóngzhào.
He repeatedly used words to incite them.
The emperor then conspired with Yè, Wénjìn, Kuāngzàn, and Yǔnmíng to kill Bīn and the others.
Once the plan was decided,
he went in to inform the Empress Dowager.
The Empress Dowager said:
"How can such a matter be undertaken lightly!
You should further discuss it with the councilors."
Yè, who was present at the time,
said:
"The late emperor once said,
'Major court affairs should not be discussed with scholars,
for their timidity leads others astray.'"
The Empress Dowager reiterated her point.
The historian notes that killing Bīn and the others was not the Empress Dowager's intention.
"Reiterated"
(pronounced fù).
"State affairs
are not for the women's quarters to know!"
He flicked his sleeves and left.
On the yǐhài day,
Yè and the others informed Yán Jìnqīng of their plot.
Jìnqīng feared the plot would not succeed.
He went to Hóngzhào's residence intending to inform him,
but Hóngzhào declined to see him due to other business.
Had Yán Jìnqīng been able to see Shǐ Hóngzhào,
then Lǐ Yè and the others would have died
without waiting for Guō Wēi's arrival.
Heaven was about to bestow power upon Guō Wēi,
so Shǐ Hóngzhào and the others died first to remove those who threatened him.
How could this be merely human affairs!
At dawn on the bǐngzǐ day,
Bīn and the others entered the court.
Several dozen armored soldiers emerged from the Guǎngzhèng Hall
and killed Bīn, Hóngzhào, and Zhāng beneath the eastern corridor.
Wénjìn urgently summoned the councilors and court officials to line up in the Chóngyuán Hall,
and proclaimed:
"Bīn and the others plotted rebellion,
and have already been executed.
I share this celebration with you, my ministers."
He also summoned the various army commanders and officers to the courtyard of the Wànsuì Hall.
According to the Wǔdài Huìyào: In the first year of the Kāipíng era of the Liáng,
the main audience hall of Biànjīng was renamed Chóngyuán Hall,
the eastern hall was renamed Xuándé Hall,
and the Wànsuì Hall was renamed Wànsuì Hall.
In the second year of the Tiānfú era of the Jìn, in the eighth month,
the Xuándé Hall was renamed Guǎngzhèng Hall.
Commander
(pronounced jiàng).
Officer
(pronounced xiào).
And he said:
"Bīn and the others regarded me as a child.
Only now have I become your true sovereign.
You are all spared from future calamities!"
They all bowed in thanks and withdrew.
He also summoned former military governors and prefects to ascend the hall for instructions,
and dispatched envoys with cavalry to arrest the relatives, associates, and attendants of Bīn and the others,
and had them all killed.
Hóngzhào had treated the Commander of the Imperial Guard Infantry, Wáng Yīn, with particular favor.
After Bīn and the others died,
the emperor sent the Palace Attendant Mèng Yè with a secret edict to Chánzhōu and Yèdū,
ordering the Zhènníng military governor Lǐ Hóngyì to kill Yīn,
and also ordering the Yèdū Field Army Cavalry Commander Guō Chóngwēi and Infantry Commander Zhēndìng's Cáo Wēi to kill Guō Wēi, the Supervisor, and the Xuānhuīshǐ Wáng Jùn.
Hóngyì
was the Empress Dowager's brother.

He also urgently issued edicts summoning the Tiānpíng military governor Gāo Xíngzhōu, the Pínglú military governor Fú Yànqīng, the Yǒngxīng military governor Guō Cóngyì, the Tàiníng military governor Mùróng Yànchāo, the Kuāngguó military governor Xuē Huáiràng, the Zhèngzhōu Defense Commissioner Wú Qiányù, and Chénzhōu Prefect Lǐ Gǔ to court.
The urgent summons of these commanders
was intended for them to bring their troops to guard the palace.
Lǐ Gǔ was merely a prefect,
yet he was also included in the number summoned to court.
This must be because his wisdom and strategies were renowned at the time.
The former Pínglú military governor Liú Zhū was appointed Acting Prefect of Kāifēng,
the Imperial Guard Cavalry Commander Lǐ Hóngjiàn was appointed Acting Manager of the Imperial Guard Bureau,
and the Palace Attendants Bureau Commissioner Yán Jìnqīng was appointed Acting Imperial Guard Cavalry Commander.
"Palace Attendants Bureau"
should be
"Inner Reception Bureau".
He was Yè's elder brother.
At that time, both inside and outside the court, people were anxious and alarmed,
alarmed that the upheaval had arisen suddenly and anxious that disaster might strike any day.
Because Hóngzhào had angrily berated Féngjí
and wanted to kill him,
he therefore hated him.
Hate
(pronounced wù).
Hearing of the upheaval, he was shocked and stunned,
and privately said to someone:
"The matter was handled too hastily.
Hasty
means rushed and not carefully considered.
It should not have come to this!"
Yè and the others ordered Liú Zhū to exterminate the families of Guō Wēi and Wáng Jùn.
Zhū was extremely cruel,
sparing not even infants or children.
Infant
means a baby.
Zhèng Xuán said: Infant
is like a fledgling.
Child
means a suckling child,
a child still drinking milk.
Hóngjiàn merely had people guard and watch over them,
and still provided them with food and drink.
On the Dīngchǒu day,
the messenger arrived at Chánzhōu.
Lǐ Hóngyì was fearful and cowardly;
concerned that Wáng Yīn already knew about the matter,
he did not dare to act.
Instead, he brought Mèng Yè to see Yīn.
Yīn imprisoned Yè
and sent Deputy Envoy Chén Guāngsuì to show the secret edict to Guō Wēi.
Wēi summoned the Bureau of Military Affairs clerk Wèi Rénpǔ
and showed him the edict, saying:
"What should I do?"
Rénpǔ said:
"You, sir,
are a great minister of the state,
your achievements and reputation have long been renowned.
Moreover, you command strong troops
and hold a strategic fortress.
If you are framed by petty men one day,
disaster will strike unexpectedly.
This cannot be resolved through mere words of explanation.
Given the current situation,
you cannot sit and wait for it."
He urged him to raise troops.
The Ouyáng History states: Wēi concealed the edict
and summoned the Bureau of Military Affairs clerk Wèi Rénpǔ to plot in his private chambers.
Rénpǔ urged Wēi to rebel,
inverted the seal of the garrison commander,
and altered the edict,
ordering Wēi to execute the various generals and officers to incite their anger.
The generals and officers all became indignant and pledged their service.
I believe the Ouyáng History must have some basis for this.
What the Comprehensive Mirror records
must be based on the Zhōu History.
The Zhōu ministers, to cover for their ruler,
also embellished the account for Wèi Rénpǔ.
He informed them of the wrongful deaths of Yáng Bīn and others and the situation regarding the secret edict,
and said:
"I, along with you all,
braved thorns and brambles,
followed the late emperor to seize the empire,
received the responsibility of being entrusted with his orphan,
and exerted all efforts to defend the state.
Now that you all have died,
how could I bear to live alone!
You should carry out the edict,
take my head to report to the Son of Heaven,
so as not to implicate you."
Guō Chóngwēi and others all wept and said:
"The Son of Heaven is young and immature.
This must be the doing of the petty men around him.
If such people achieve their ambitions,
how can the state be at peace!
Chóngwēi wishes to follow you, sir, to the court to plead your case,
to sweep away these rats and cleanse the court.
You must not be killed by a single messenger,
bearing an evil name for a thousand years."
The Hanlin astronomer Zhào Xiūjǐ said to Guō Wēi:
"What good is it for you, sir, to die in vain!
It would be better to follow the will of the masses,
lead the troops south,
this is Heaven's revelation."
Zhào Xiūjǐ advised Lǐ Shǒuzhēn but urged Guō Wēi,
confident in his own methods.
He ordered Guō Chóngwēi to lead the cavalry as the vanguard.
On the Wùyín day,
he personally led the main army to follow.
Meanwhile, Mùróng Yànchāo was eating
when he received the edict.
He put down his spoon and chopsticks and entered the court.
The emperor entrusted all military affairs to him.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: From Yǎnzhōu to Dàliáng is six hundred lǐ.
Mùróng Yànchāo arrived in three days,
believing that as the late emperor's sibling,
he urgently rushed to the court,
unaware that his talent and wisdom were insufficient to succeed.
On the Jǐmǎo day,
Wú Qiányù entered the court.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: From Zhèngzhōu to Dàliáng is one hundred and forty lǐ.
The emperor heard that Guō Wēi was leading troops southward
and discussed sending troops to resist him.
The former Kāifēng Prefect Hóu Yì said:
"The families of the garrison troops from Yèdū are all in the capital.
The imperial army should not lightly venture out.
It would be better to close the city gates to blunt their advance,
and have their mothers and wives ascend the walls to summon them.
Then they could be subdued without fighting."
Mùróng Yànchāo said:
"Hóu Yì is old and feeble,
proposing a coward's plan."
The emperor then sent Yì, along with Yán Jìnqīng, Wú Qiányù, and former Bǎodà Military Commissioner Zhāng Yànchāo, to lead the imperial guards toward Chánzhōu.
On that day,
Guō Wēi had already reached Chánzhōu.
From Wèizhōu south to Chánzhōu is one hundred and fifty lǐ;
he arrived in two days,
intending to catch the Hàn unprepared.
Wáng Yīn welcomed him with a tearful audience
and followed Guō Wēi across the river with his troops.
The emperor sent the eunuch Luò Tuō to spy on Guō Wēi.
Wēi captured him
and placed a memorial inside Luò Tuō's collar,
sending him back to report to the emperor:
"Your subject recently received the edict
and awaited death with bated breath.
Guō Chóngwēi and others could not bear to kill me,
saying that this was all due to slander by those around Your Majesty who are greedy for power and insatiable.
They forced me to travel south,
to come to the court and plead guilty.
I sought death but could not obtain it,
and lacked the strength to control them.
I will arrive at the court in a few days.
If Your Majesty considers me guilty,
how dare I escape punishment!
If there truly are those who slandered me,
I hope they can be handed over to the army to satisfy the masses.
Then I dare not fail to pacify the troops
and withdraw back to Yèdū!"
On the Gēngchén day,
Guō Wēi headed toward Huázhōu.
From Chánzhōu southwest to Huázhōu is over one hundred lǐ.
Qù,
pronounced qī yù fān.
On the Xīnsì day,
Yìchéng Military Commissioner Sòng Yánwò welcomed and surrendered.
Examination of discrepancies: The Shílù of Emperor Yǐn states:
"In the eleventh month,
on the Bǐngzǐ day,
Yáng and Shǐ were executed.
On the Dīngchǒu day,
Mèng Yè arrived at Chánzhōu.
Wáng Yīn imprisoned Yè and sent him to Guō Wēi,
setting out that same day.
On the Wùyín day,
he reached the river,
and met Wáng Yīn.
On the Gēngchén day,
he encamped at Huázhōu."
The Shílù of Emperor Tàizǔ of Zhōu states:
"On the thirteenth day,
at night,
Tàizǔ dreamed of entering the court for an audience.
At dawn,
he showed the dream to Jùn.
On that day,
Chén Hóngsuì arrived at Yèdū."
This was the fourteenth day, Dīngchǒu.
The next day,
he was forced by the masses to take the road,
which was the fifteenth day, Wùyín.
The following day,
while traveling,
he encountered Luò Tuō
and intended to stay at Chánzhōu,
which was the sixteenth day, Jǐmǎo.
The text below also states:
"On the sixteenth day, he headed toward Huátái."
According to this, from Dàliáng to Chánzhōu is two hundred and seventy lǐ,
from Chánzhōu to Yèdū is one hundred and forty lǐ,
and to Huázhōu is one hundred and twenty lǐ.
It is unlikely that the round trip could be made so quickly.
The Shílù of Hàn and Zhōu differ on the departure date and the arrival at Huázhōu.
It seems that on the sixteenth day, he headed toward Huázhōu,
and arrived at Huázhōu on the seventeenth day.
Now, I follow the Shílù of Emperor Tàizǔ of Zhōu.
He was a man of Luòyáng,
and his wife was the Yǒngníng Princess, daughter of Emperor Gāozǔ of Jìn.
Guō Wēi took supplies from the Huázhōu treasury to reward the officers and soldiers,
and addressed them, saying:
"I have heard that Lord Hóu has already led the various armies from the south.
Hóu Yì also held the title of Zhōngshū Lìng,
hence he is referred to as Lord.
If we engage in battle, it would contradict the purpose of entering the court.
If we do not fight, we will be slaughtered by them.
I wish to preserve your achievements and reputations,
so it would be better to carry out the previous edict.
I would die without regret!"
Guō Wēi said this to gauge the loyalty of the masses.
"The state has wronged you, sir,
but you have not wronged the state.
That is why ten thousand men strive fervently,
as if avenging a personal enemy.
What can Hóu Yì and his ilk do!"
Wáng Jùn announced to the masses:
"I have received instructions from the Duke:
once we capture the capital,
you are permitted to plunder for ten days."
The masses all leaped for joy.
On the Xīnsì day,
the Lóngtuō (messenger) arrived at Dàliáng.
Prior to this, the Emperor had discussed personally going to Chánzhōu,
but upon hearing that Guō Wēi had already reached the river, he stopped.
The Emperor wore a deeply regretful and fearful expression,
and privately said to Dòu Zhēngù:
"Recently, things have been too hasty."
Lǐ Yè and others requested emptying the treasury to reward the armies.
Sū Yùguī believed it was inadvisable.
Lǐ Yè bowed to Yùguī before the Emperor,
and said:
"Your Excellency, for the sake of the Son of Heaven, do not begrudge the treasury!"
Thus, each soldier of the Imperial Guard was given twenty strings of cash,
the lower armies half that amount,
and families of officers and men in the north were provided for,
to allow communication with their families and entice them.
On the Rénwǔ day,
Guō Wēi's army reached Fēngqiū,
and public sentiment was filled with fear and alarm.
The Empress Dowager wept and said:
"Not heeding Lǐ Tāo's words,
it is fitting that we perish!"
(Lǐ Tāo's words
are recorded in the first year of the previous volume.)
She said to the Emperor:
"In my view, the northern army is like mere gnats."
(Erya Commentary: Mièměng [gnats/midges],
are born from damp, dark places,
also called xījī [vinegar flies].
Sūn Yán said: These insects are tiny and fly in swarms.
Liezi says: Mièměng are born on decaying soil,
come to life with rain,
and die upon seeing the sun.
Zhuangzi calls them xījī.
Miè,
pronounced mòjié fān.
Měng,
pronounced mòkǒng fān.)
He retreated,
saw Niè Wénjìn,
asked about the number of northern troops and the names of their commanders,
became quite fearful,
and said:
"These are also formidable rebels,
not to be taken lightly!"

The Emperor again dispatched Left Shenwu Commander-in-Chief Yuán Shānyì, former Weishèng Jiedushi Liú Zhòngjìn, and others to lead the Imperial Guard to join Hóu Yì and others, assembling and encamping at Chìgāng.
(Shānyì
was the son of Xiàngxiān.)
Mùróng Yànchāo stationed his main army at Qīlǐdiàn.
On the Guǐwèi day,
the southern and northern armies met at Liúzǐbēi.
(Liúzǐbēi is south of Fēngqiū,
north of the Biàn suburbs.)
The Empress Dowager said:
"Guō Wēi is an old acquaintance of our family.
Unless death were imminent,
why would he come to this!
We should merely hold our troops and guard the city,
swiftly send an edict to instruct him,
observe his intentions.
He will surely have reasons to explain himself.
Then the rites between ruler and minister can still be preserved.
Be careful not to go out lightly."
The Emperor did not listen.
(Had the Emperor heeded the Empress Dowager's words,
although he might not have been able to secure his former position,
he would not have met his death in the wilds.)
The Empress Dowager sent a messenger to warn Niè Wénjìn, saying:
"You must be extremely careful!"
He replied:
"With your servant here,
even if there were a hundred Guō Wēis,
they could be captured!"
By evening,
the two armies did not engage in battle,
and the Emperor returned to the palace.
Mùróng Yànchāo boasted:
"If Your Majesty has no matters in the palace tomorrow,
I hope you will come out again to watch your servant defeat the rebels.
I need not even fight them,
but can simply shout to scatter them and make them return to camp!"
On the Jiǎshēn day,
the Emperor wished to go out again.
The Empress Dowager strenuously tried to stop him,
but he would not listen.
Once the formations were drawn up,
Guō Wēi cautioned his troops, saying:
"I have come to punish the petty villains,
not to oppose the Son of Heaven.
Be careful not to act first."
After a long time,
Mùróng Yànchāo led light cavalry straight forward in a fierce attack.
Guō Chóngwēi and former Bózhōu Cìshǐ Lǐ Róng led cavalry to resist him.
Yànchāo's horse fell,
and he was nearly captured.
Yànchāo led his troops in retreat,
with over a hundred of his subordinates dead.
Thereupon, the morale of the various armies broke,
and they gradually surrendered to the northern army.
Hóu Yì, Wú Qiānyù, Zhāng Yànchāo, Yuán Shānyì, and Liú Zhòngjìn all secretly went to see Guō Wēi.
Wēi sent each back to their camps,
and also said to Sòng Yánwò:
"The Son of Heaven is in danger.
You are a close relative,
you should take your personal troops to guard the imperial carriage.
Also, convey a memorial to His Majesty,
hoping he will seize an early opportunity to come to my camp."
(Sòng Yánwò
was the emperor's son-in-law,
hence called a close relative.
Personal troops refers to the Yìchéng personal troops under Yánwò's command.
Guard the carriage,
pronounced shéngzhèng fān.
Opportunity,
pronounced gǔxiàn fān.)
The chaotic soldiers swarmed like clouds,
and he dared not advance and returned.
By dusk,
most of the southern army had gone over to the north.
Mùróng Yànchāo fled back to Yǎnzhōu with a dozen or so horsemen from his command.
That evening,
the Emperor alone, with the three chancellors and several dozen attendants, spent the night at Qīlǐzhài,
while all the others fled and scattered.
(The three chancellors: Dòu Zhēngù, Sū Féngjí, Yùguī.
Qīlǐzhài
is the Qīlǐdiàn camp where Mùróng Yànchāo was stationed.)
On the Yǐyǒu day,
Guō Wēi, looking from afar, saw the Son of Heaven's banners on a high slope.
He dismounted, removed his helmet, and went to join him,
but upon arrival, the Emperor had already left.
The Emperor urged his horse to return to the palace.
Arriving at Xuánhuà Gate,
(Xuánhuà Gate
is the first gate from the east on the north side of Dàliáng city wall.
Originally called Suānzǎo Gate,
in the first year of Liáng Kāipíng it was renamed Xìnghé Gate,
and in the third year of Jìn Tiānfù it was renamed Xuánhuà Gate.)
he asked the Emperor's attendants:
"Where are the troops?"
Then he shot at the attendants.
The Emperor turned his horse's reins,
went northwest to Zhàocūn,
but pursuing troops had already arrived.
The Emperor dismounted and entered a commoner's house,
where he was assassinated by chaotic soldiers.
(Textual analysis says: According to the Veritable Records:
"The Emperor arrived at Xuánhuà Gate,
Liú Zhū shot at the Emperor's attendants,
the Emperor turned towards the northwest,
Guō Yǔnmíng followed behind with bared blade.
Northwest to Zhàocūn,
the vanguard had already caught up,
chaotic soldiers seethed and boiled,
the Emperor, afraid,
dismounted and entered a commoner's house.
Guō Yǔnmíng, knowing the situation was hopeless,
then drew his blade, violated the imperial presence, and the Emperor perished."
The Old History of the Five Dynasties, Annals of Emperor Yǐn:
"Guō Yǔnmíng, knowing the situation was hopeless,
then stabbed the Emperor with his blade, and the Emperor perished.
Yǔnmíng committed suicide."
Annals of Tàizǔ of Zhōu says:
"Yǔnmíng assassinated the Hàn Emperor at the northern suburbs."
Liú Shù said:
"Yǔnmíng was trusted and favored by the Emperor;
why would he commit regicide!
It is likely Guō Wēi's troops killed the Emperor.
After the deed was done, they concealed it,
and because Yǔnmíng committed suicide, they blamed him."
The assassin of the Emperor was likely not Yǔnmíng,
but no one knows who it was,
hence it is only said 'chaotic soldiers'.)
Niè Wénjìn fled alone,
and soldiers pursued and beheaded him.
Lǐ Yè fled to Shǎnzhōu.
(Jiǔyù Zhì: From Dàliáng to Shǎnzhōu is 659 lǐ.
Lǐ Yè wished to rely on his elder brother.
Shǎn,
pronounced shīrǎn fān.)
He wished to rely on Mùróng Yànchāo.
He wailed and lamented, saying:
"It is this old man's fault!"
Guō Wēi arrived at Xuánhuà Gate,
and Liú Zhū shot arrows like rain outside the city walls.
(Shooting like rain means shooting arrows like rain.)
He returned to his private residence.
(Yíngchūn Gate
is the first gate from the north on the east side of the Biàn city wall.
Originally called Cáomén,
in the first year of Liáng Kāipíng it was renamed Jiànyáng Gate,
and in the third year of Jìn Tiānfù it was renamed Yíngchūn Gate.)
The various armies plundered extensively,
and throughout the night, fires and smoke arose from all directions.
Soldiers entered the former residence of Bái Zàiróng, the military governor of Yìchéng,
seized Zàiróng,
and plundered all his wealth.
Afterward, they stepped forward and said:
"We once served under your command,
yet now we have acted so disrespectfully toward you.
How could we face you again!"
They then cut off his head and left.
Considering Bái Zàiróng's cruelty in Zhēndìng,
his suffering this calamity now
may indeed be the work of Heaven's justice.
刎 (wěn),
pronounced as in 武粉翻 (wǔ fěn fān).
The Vice Minister of Personnel, Zhāng Yǔn,
had family assets worth tens of thousands,
but he was extremely miserly.
Not even his wife was entrusted with them;
he often tied all the keys to his belt beneath his clothes,
and they jingled like jade ornaments as he walked.
That evening,
he hid above the caisson ceiling in the Buddhist hall.
According to the Fēngsú Tōng, the hall's ceiling was modeled after the Eastern Well constellation,
carved with lotus and water chestnut patterns;
lotus and water chestnuts are aquatic plants,
used to ward off fire.
Dù Yòu said: In Hàn palaces, ceilings were generally called "wells,"
all painted with water plants, lotuses, and caltrops to ward off fire.
Hé Yàn's "Ode to the Jǐngfú Palace" states:
"Adorned with caisson ceilings,
arranged with intricate patterns."
Also, Wáng Wénkǎo's "Ode to the Língguāng Palace" says:
"Round pools and square wells,
with lotuses and algae planted upside down."
This refers to square wells painted with algae patterns above.
Lù Dián's Pǐyǎ states: The rafters covering the roof
are called caisson ceilings.
The plank broke, and he fell.
Soldiers stripped him of his clothes,
and he froze to death.
Earlier,
the Workshop Commissioner Jiǎ Yánhuī was favored by the Emperor,
and he lived next to Wèi Rénpǔ.
He wanted to annex Rénpǔ's residence to expand his own,
and repeatedly slandered Rénpǔ to the Emperor,
nearly causing Rénpǔ's death.
This means he almost died.
几 (jī),
pronounced as in 居依翻 (jū yī fān).
Someone captured Yánhuī and handed him over to Rénpǔ,
but Rénpǔ declined, saying:
"To seek revenge amidst chaos
is something I will not do!"
Guō Wēi heard of this
and treated Rénpǔ with even greater respect.
The Grand General of the Right Thousand Bull Guard, Zǎoqiáng's Zhào Fèng, said:
"Guō, the Palace Attendant, raised troops
to eliminate the wicked around the sovereign and bring peace to the state.
Yet these petty men dare to act like this—
they are nothing but bandits!
How could this be the Palace Attendant's intention?"
He took up his bow and arrows,
sat on a folding chair,
and positioned himself at the head of the lane.
Whenever looters approached,
he shot and killed them.
Thus, the entire neighborhood was preserved.
On Bǐngxū,
Liú Shū and Lǐ Hóngjiàn were captured
and imprisoned.
The Kǎoyì states: According to the Wǔdài Shǐ Quēwén:
"When Zhōu's ancestor raised troops from Yè,
Shū slaughtered all of Zhōu's ancestor's family—dozens of children and women—
with extreme cruelty.
After the Hidden Emperor was killed,
Zhōu's ancestor, under the Hàn Empress Dowager's order, imprisoned Shū
and sent someone to reprimand him,
asking why he killed his family.
Shū replied: 'I was merely executing a traitor's clan for the Hàn house,
nothing more.'
Wēi was enraged
and killed him."
Wáng Yǔchēng said:
"During the reign of Zhōu Shìzōng,
when historians compiled the Hidden Emperor's Veritable Records,
Shū's loyal words were omitted and not recorded.
Shū now has a son, Xiàohé,
who passed the imperial examinations."
However, Shū was known for his greed and cruelty wherever he served.
In Qīngzhōu, he plotted to resist his replacement,
and only after Guō Qióng persuaded him
did he enter the court.
He harbored personal grudges against Yáng and Shǐ,
rejoicing at their executions.
When the Hidden Emperor fled back,
Shū shot at him and refused him entry,
leaving him to die in the wild.
His massacre of Zhōu's ancestor's family
stemmed from his cruel nature—
how could he be considered a loyal and righteous man?
What Wáng Yǔchēng recorded
likely relied on Xiàohé's words.
It is not adopted here.
"After I die,
will you become someone's servant?"
His wife replied:
"Given your actions,
it is only fitting!"
Wáng Yīn and Guō Chóngwēi said to Guō Wēi:
"If the looting is not stopped,
by tonight only an empty city will remain."
Wēi then ordered his generals to divide and patrol to stop the looters,
executing those who disobeyed.
By late afternoon,
order was restored.
Dòu Zhèngù and Sū Yǔguī fled back from Qīlǐzhài.
Guō Wēi sent people to find them,
and they were soon reinstated to their positions.
While Zhèngù served as chancellor,
Yáng and Shǐ wielded power arbitrarily.
(Yáng Bīn and Shǐ Hóngzhào.)
He merely maintained a dignified composure among them,
preserving himself.
Guō Wēi ordered officials to move the Hidden Emperor's coffin to the Western Palace.
Some suggested following the precedent of Wèi's Duke Gāoguìxiāng,
burying him with ducal rites.
(The Duke Gāoguìxiāng incident is recorded in the sixty-seventh scroll of Wèi Yuándì's Jǐngyuán first year.)
Wēi said:
"In the haste of the moment,
I failed to protect the imperial carriage—
my crime is already grave.
How dare I further demean the sovereign!"
The Grand Preceptor Féng Dào led the officials to pay respects to Guō Wēi.
When Wēi saw him,
he still bowed to him.
Dào accepted the bow as usual.
The Kǎoyì states: According to the Wǔdài Shǐ Quēwén:
"When Zhōu's ancestor entered the capital,
the officials paid him respects.
Zhōu's ancestor still bowed when he saw Dào,
expecting Dào to immediately support his enthronement.
But Dào accepted the bow as usual
and slowly said: 'Palace Attendant, this journey of yours was not easy!'
Zhōu's ancestor's spirits dampened,
so his plan for the throne was delayed."
However, after Zhōu's ancestor raised troops and captured the capital,
the reason he did not immediately become emperor
was because the Hàn imperial clan members—Chóng in Hédōng,
Xìn in Xǔzhōu,
and Yūn in Xúzhōu—
if he hastily replaced the Hàn,
feared these three garrisons would raise troops under the pretext of restoration,
and both inside and outside there would surely be responses.
Therefore, he outwardly claimed to support establishing an imperial son.
Xìn was always mediocre and foolish,
not worth fearing;
Yūn was Chóng's son,
so he welcomed Yūn and established him,
pacifying the two garrisons' schemes.
Once Yūn had left Xúzhōu far behind,
and was closer to the capital,
he then eliminated Xìn as well,
thus removing two of the three garrisons.
Only then did he proclaim himself emperor,
leaving only Chóng as his enemy.
This was his strategy—
how could it be thwarted by Féng Dào accepting a bow?
Dào accepted the bow as usual
precisely to demonstrate his dignified composure.
"Palace Attendant, this journey of yours was not easy!"
On the Dīnghài day,
Guō Wēi led the officials to the Míngdé Gate to inquire after the Empress Dowager's well-being,
and memorialized:
"Military and state affairs are pressing,
we request the early establishment of an heir apparent."
The Empress Dowager issued an edict stating:
"Guō Yǔnmíng committed regicide and rebellion,
the Empress Dowager's edict says so,
it was Guō Wēi's intention.
The Examination of Discrepancies has already debated this earlier.
Hédōng military governor Chóng,
Zhōngwǔ military governor Xìn,
are both brothers of Gāozǔ,
Wǔníng military governor Yūn,
Kāifēng prefect Xūn,
are sons of Gāozǔ,
let the officials deliberate and choose who is appropriate."
Yūn,
was the son of Chóng,
Gāozǔ loved him,
and raised him as his own son.
Lù Zhèn's *History of the Nine States*: Liú Chóng's eldest son was Yūn,
clever and cunning from a young age,
Gāozǔ pitied him,
and registered him as his own son.
Yūn,
pronunciation according to Yúlún.
According to the *Old History of the Five Dynasties*,
in the second year of Tóngguāng of Táng Zhuāngzōng,
the Empress Dowager's palace was renamed Chángshòu Palace,
the Jìn and Hàn probably called it Wànsuì Palace.
Some say: it was named after the Wànsuì Hall.
See,
pronunciation Xiánbiàn.
The Empress Dowager said:
"Xūn has long been ill and weak, unable to rise."
Guō Wēi went out to inform the generals,
the generals requested to see him,
the Empress Dowager ordered attendants to carry him on a couch to show the generals,
and only then did the generals believe it.
Thereupon, Guō Wēi and Jùn discussed establishing Yūn.
On the Jǐchǒu day,
Guō Wēi led the officials in submitting a memorial requesting that Yūn inherit the great lineage.
The Empress Dowager ordered the relevant offices,
to select a date,
and prepare the imperial carriage to welcome Yūn to ascend the throne.
Guō Wēi memorialized to send Grand Preceptor Féng Dào and Privy Council Academician Wáng Dù, and Palace Library Director Zhào Shàngjiāo to Xúzhōu to respectfully welcome him.
*Examination of Discrepancies* says: The *Veritable Records of Zhōu Tàizǔ*:
"On the Jǐchǒu day,
Tàizǔ memorialized to send former Grand Preceptor Féng Dào there to convey the decree.
Tàizǔ was about to submit a memorial to Xúzhōu,
unsure whom to send,
Privy Council Academician Wáng Dù requested to go,
and was permitted.
The chief ministers and all officials memorialized that Palace Library Director Zhào Shàngjiāo would carry the edict and set out on the same day."
*Missing Texts of the History of the Five Dynasties*:
"Zhōu Zǔ requested Dào to go to Xúzhōu,
to enfeoff the Duke of Xiāngyīn as the Hàn heir.
Dào said: 'Is the Palace Attendant sincere?'
Zhōu Zǔ swore an oath.
Dào said: 'Do not make this old man a liar.'
When he departed,
he said to people: 'In all my life I have never lied,
now I have become a liar.'"
Wáng Yǔchēng said:
"During the reign of Zhōu Shìzōng,
an edict ordered historians to compile the *Veritable Records of Zhōu Zǔ*,
therefore Dào's deeds,
should be concealed."
Considering Dào was honest and wise, preserving himself,
feigning foolishness to avoid disaster,
he probably would not have dared to provoke Zhōu Zǔ's undisclosed intentions,
later people wanted to praise him and thus said this.
Also, the *Veritable Records of Emperor Yǐn* says:
"Initially, when discussing establishing the Xúzhōu commander,
the Empress Dowager sent a palace envoy to swiftly inform Liú Chóng,
requesting Chóng to enter and succeed to the great position.
Chóng, knowing his son was being established,
submitted a memorial declining modestly."
I fear there was no such event.
Now it is not adopted.
